In a fiscal conundrum. Pakistan’s fiscal position in FY26 presents a paradox: apparent stability that masks deep-seated fragility. While the overall fiscal deficit narrowed to 1.6 per cent of GDP during the first 11 months (July-May) — with the July-April period falling to 1.1pc — this achievement rests on fragile foundations. Total public debt stood at a staggering Rs83.29 trillion ($298.5 billion) by the end of March 2026, while interest payments consumed Rs6.16tr in just 11 months. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects a fiscal deficit of 3.2pc for FY27. With the Federal Board of Revenue missing its IMF tax target by Rs975bn and debt servicing crowding out development spending, the country walks a fiscal tightrope — stabilisation today, sustainability tomorrow remains an open question. While headline fiscal indicators suggest some macroeconomic stabilisation, the underlying pressures become far clearer when one examines the power sector. Capacity payments, circular debt and costly contractual obligations have emerged among the largest structural drivers of the country’s fiscal stress. The defining feature of many Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) is the capacity payment mechanism. Under these contracts, power producers receive fixed payments to recover capital costs, debt servicing and fixed operating expenses regardless of whether electricity is generated. The economy has reached a stage where structural reforms can no longer be postponed Consumers therefore pay not only for electricity consumed but also for maintaining power plants that may remain idle for years. As installed capacity expanded faster than electricity demand, these fixed obligations became one of the largest components of electricity tariffs. The financial burden is immense. During FY25, Pakistani consumers paid approximately Rs 1.81tr in capacity charges — around Rs 14.3 per unit — while actual energy costs amounted to only Rs9 per unit. Capacity payments accounted for nearly 61pc of the total electricity bill of Rs2.94tr. Projections for 2026 indicate capacity charges of around Rs 1.7tr, equivalent to roughly Rs17 per unit. The burden is compounded by dollar-indexed returns embedded in many early Independent Power Producers (IPP) contracts . Although these guarantees attracted much-needed private investment, they also exposed Pakistan to exchange-rate risk, with every depreciation of the rupee automatically increasing government payment obligations. Projects developed under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) illustrate this vulnerability. More than 11,000 megawatts of installed capacity were financed largely in foreign currency, while receivables owed to CPEC-related IPPs have reportedly reached Rs543bn, adding further pressure to public finances. These contractual obligations have become a major driver of Pakistan’s circular debt. When distribution companies fail to recover the full cost of electricity because of transmission losses, theft, poor recoveries and delayed subsidies, payments to power producers are postponed. The resulting liabilities accumulate across the supply chain, forcing repeated government borrowing simply to keep the sector operational. Although the government reduced circular debt from Rs2.39tr to Rs1.61tr during FY25 through extraordinary financial interventions, the improvement proved temporary. By the close of FY26, circular debt had climbed back to approximately Rs1.84tr, well above the IMF target. Recognising the severity of the challenge, the government renegotiated contracts with fourteen IPPs in January 2025, replacing parts of the traditional “take-or-pay” model with arrangements more closely linked to actual electricity generation. These revisions are expected to generate lifetime savings of approximately Rs1.4tr, while settling returns on equity in Pakistani rupees instead of open-ended dollar indexation marks another important reform. However, the largest challenge remains unresolved. CPEC-related IPPs still account for roughly Rs1.4tr in outstanding receivables and continue to dominate the circular debt equation. Until these liabilities are comprehensively addressed, durable fiscal relief is likely to remain elusive. Pakistan’s challenge is therefore not the existence of IPPs but the design of contracts that balance investor confidence with fiscal sustainability. Without a comprehensive overhaul of power-sector governance and future PPAs, the IPP model will continue to weigh heavily on public finances. Yet energy-sector reform alone cannot restore long-term fiscal sustainability. Our broader fiscal challenge also stems from weaknesses in the intergovernmental fiscal framework, making federal-provincial resource sharing and fiscal governance the next critical area for structural reform. Pakistan’s fiscal architecture has reached a stage where structural reforms can no longer be postponed. While the 18th Constitutional Amendment and the 7th National Finance Commission (NFC) Award fundamentally reshaped the country’s federal system by devolving greater powers and financial resources to the provinces, questions remain over whether the existing framework is delivering better public services and sustainable public finances. These concerns are central to the World Bank’s report , Strengthening Fiscal Federalism in Pakistan, released last month. The report argues that although devolution brought government closer to citizens, Pakistan’s fiscal system has struggled to keep pace with changing administrative responsibilities, resulting in persistent fiscal imbalances, fragmented taxation and uneven service delivery. Following the report’s release, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif constituted a high-level committee to review its recommendations in consultation with provincial governments and other stakeholders. The report does not advocate reversing devolution; rather, it proposes reforms to make Pakistan’s federal system more efficient, accountable and development-oriented. Governance failures. AN effort is underway to spark a debate on creating new administrative units in the country ostensibly on the grounds that the present system is not delivering. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whose proximity to the establishment is well known, tried to make the case . Claiming the present governance system has “collapsed”, he called for more provinces and administrative units. He offered no explanation of what “collapse” meant and how new units would magically fix Pakistan’s problems. His proposal found backing from the military spokesman . He echoed the call, urged a system “reset” and endorsed the creation of new administrative units. Such calls are, of course, not new. Every so often, this proposal surfaces, mostly from the establishment or other interested groups. But any sweeping change has never found traction among major political parties or the public at large. This time was no different. Naqvi faced criticism from across the political spectrum. Prominent ruling party leaders questioned his statement. The PPP’s Sindh chief minister, Murad Ali Shah, roundly rejected the creation of new provinces. Awami Tehreek leaders accused the interior minister of advocating Sindh’s division. Other parties argued that an “illegitimate” government had no authority to undertake such a move. The Lahore High Court Bar Association condemned Naqvi’s proposal as unconstitutional. Its office-bearers said those responsible for the destruction of the existing order were now proposing a “new system”. The argument that Pakistan’s governance crisis is due to the number or size of its provinces simply doesn’t hold. One can make a case for administrative reorganisation on other grounds. For example, smaller units can bring government closer to the people. But that goal can be achieved by empowering local government. In any case, the Constitution lays out a clear process for making any changes to provinces. Naqvi’s proposal implied it can be done by executive fiat. Any change including altering the boundary of any province requires a resolution passed by a two-thirds majority in the relevant provincial assembly, followed by a constitutional amendment adopted by a two-thirds majority in both the National Assembly and Senate. The timing of this debate is baffling. The debate is being initiated at a time when one province confronts an active insurgency, a second faces mounting militant violence, and Azad Kashmir is experiencing widespread protests and civil unrest. There is a spurious connection between the provincial configuration and the governance crisis. Those who draw a spurious link between Pakistan’s provincial structure and its governance failures lack historical perspective of why the country today is beset with so many serious, overlapping challenges. These challenges are the cumulative result of prolonged political instability, deferred economic reforms, visionless leadership, rule without law, and a consistent preference by successive governments for foreign engagements over unresolved, festering domestic problems. External overreach and internal underreach has been a consistent pattern. Governance is adversely affected by these factors. But it is elite capture that has been the most damaging. Elite control of state power, of politics and much of the country’s resources has ensured elite interests consistently trump public interests. The power elite — a symbiotic nexus between political and military actors — has resisted meaningful reform and avoided tackling the economy’s structural problems — tax reforms, land reforms, reforms in governance. It has ‘rentier’ characteristics: using access to public office to leverage state resources for its own gain. Elite capture is principally why governance has broken down. This has left the country with interlocking crisis: state insolvency, insecurity, poverty, crumbling education and health systems, mounting energy shortages as well as environmental degradation. At the same time, the convergence between the country’s youth bulge, economic stagnation and the education deficit poses stark risks for the future. A closer look at Pakistan’s governance failures shows political instability to be the core driver. The country has lurched between military interventions and civilian rule in a recurring cycle, punctuated by outbreaks of public protests demanding political change. This political discontinuity has prevented the emergence of a stable and predictable environment in which to address the country’s problems. It also entrenched a power asymmetry between elected and unelected institutions. In recent years, this produced a hybrid model of informal power-sharing between the civilian government and the military. That arrangement has now been supplanted by military dominance. A major contributor to present challenges has been the persistent reliance by both civilian and military governments on dysfunctional and unsustainable economic policies. Rather than mobilise domestic resources, successive governments turned to borrowing and bailouts to cover widening budget and balance-of-payments deficits — the root of chronic financial crises. The country’s foreign alignments ensured steady access to economic aid and external funds. This ‘borrowed growth’ might have worked if the fiscal space had been used to fix structural problems. It wasn’t. Instead, external financing, combined with high remittances, allowed ruling elites to paper over those problems and avoid reform. The failure to raise adequate domestic resources together with low levels of savings and investment led to increased borrowing and higher debt. This resulted in an economy that lurches from one IMF tranche to the next. Today Pakistan is stuck in a low-growth, low-investment, high-debt equilibrium trap that clouds its economic future. But the power elite refuses to change course. Governance challenges have also been compounded by the repercussions of protracted foreign engagements, the dynamics of great power competition, and the fault lines of regional geopolitics. An implacably hostile India, unresolved Kashmir dispute, and an unstable Afghanistan pushed security to the top of the national agenda. But this involved a strategic trade-off. Defence spending and objectives were prioritised at the expense of economic development, social services and broader policy goals. Elite interests, flawed policies, failure to reform, chronic instability and the headwinds from geopolitical storms are all drivers of Pakistan’s governance crisis. It is not the number of provinces or the administrative architecture that are the source of the crisis. Improvements in provincial efficiency and delivery are certainly needed. But to justify altering the Constitution’s provincial framework using disingenuous arguments does no service to the country. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Ten more placed on Fourth Schedule in Azad Kashmir. MIRPUR: The Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) government has placed 10 more residents of the region on the Fourth Schedule of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 2014, over their alleged affiliation with the proscribed Jammu and Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JK-JAAC), according to an official notification. Placement on the Fourth Schedule subjects individuals to monitoring by law-enforcement agencies and may involve legal restrictions relating to movement, political and organisational activities, foreign travel and financial transactions. According to the AJK Home Department notification, the decision was taken in light of a resolution adopted at the AJK cabinet meeting held on June 5. The AJK President, exercising powers under Section 16(1) of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 2014, approved the inclusion of the 10 individuals on the Fourth Schedule. Tick, tick ... boom. IN hindsight, revolutions are easy to predict. Years, decades and even centuries after such events, scholars will write volumes explaining how prevailing conditions made such violent action inevitable, with the most common preconditions being extreme economic inequality and injustice along with an oppressive state which is not only prone to overreaction but is also so wedded to using force that it has forgotten all other means of conflict reduction and resolution. What is next to impossible to predict is the single spark that sets off the explosion, the final straw that breaks the back of the ancient regime. And all too often, that spark is so small as to be insignificant and the straw is almost weightless compared to the existing burden accumulated over years. In Bangladesh, the issue of job reservations led to the swift end of Hasina Wajed’s 15-year reign and resulted in her fleeing the country, but how many jobs were actually reserved this way? According to most calculations, they were no more than 1,000 at most and given Bangladesh’s population and relative economic prosperity one would imagine that this would have been a relatively minor issue. Certainly, Hasina Wajed — with the overconfidence and isolation that absolute power breeds — thought it would blow over. Instead, it blew her regime away. Similarly, in Nepal, while anger over widespread political corruption, high unemployment and extreme economic inequality and frustration was the norm, the spark that led ‘Gen Z’ to riot was the government’s September 2025 ban on 26 social media platforms. While the government framed this as a regulatory measure, the protesters were convinced that the real reason for the ban was to block a social media trend that focused on the privileges and wealth of the children and close relatives of Nepal’s ruling class. The economic divide had always been a reality, but now, for the first time, a poor unemployed youngster in Nepal could see the sons and daughters of ministers live it up on Instagram, spending more on a single purchase than that youth could hope to earn in a lifetime. By the time states get around to addressing the spark, the fire has spread. In Bangladesh, Hasina Wajed got the supreme court to reduce the reservation quota to seven per cent but it was too little, too late; the fuse had already been lit and the protests had become an uprising against authoritarianism and the loss of life during the government crackdown. Ensconced in her palace, one imagines that Hasina simply didn’t understand what had hit her. A single spark can set off an explosion. In Nepal the government lifted the social media ban just a few days after imposing it but by that time several dozen protesters had been killed and government buildings set on fire. Four days after the ban was imposed, and one day after it was lifted, the prime minister had to resign. India’s ‘cockroach’ movement was milder in comparison. However, it represented not just anger at exam leaks but a deeper frustration with a system seemingly fully captured by the Sangh agenda and networks. Despite the state’s surprise that time-tested heavy-handed tactics and media smears no longer seemed to work, it acted with far more foresight than its neighbours by addressing the central demands before the movement spread out of control and by not resorting to deadly force. The final fate of the movement remains to be decided, but for now, it seems the crisis has passed even though it exposed the chinks in Narendra Modi’s hitherto impenetrable armour. Often, state overreaction to a movement or protest causes that protest to balloon into rebellion and revolution even if that was not the original intention of the demonstrators. Case in point: a large but mostly peaceful procession of peasant workers led by Orthodox priest Father Georgy Gapon on Jan 9, 1905. Gapon was no revolutionary and nor were revolutionary elements prominent in the crowd. In fact, anti-tsar parties like the Bolsheviks had disapproved of the march due to its lack of political demands. Carrying icons and portraits of the tsar, the crowd regarded Nicholas II as their benevolent ‘little father’ whom, they hoped, would listen to their pleas and save them from exploitation. Instead, the crowd was fired upon by panicked imperial troops resulting in hundreds of deaths. Distraught and dismayed, surrounded by the dead and wounded, the previously pro-tsar Gapon was heard to shout: “There is no God any longer. There is no tsar.” And from here on, the days of imperial Russia were numbered. Here then are lessons for all states, inc­luding our own: address concerns before they metastasize beyond treatment and just because a strategy has worked in the past there is no guarantee that it will not backfire in the present. Finally, never use a hacksaw when a scalpel is required. The writer is a journalist. X: @zarrarkhuhro Published in Dawn, August 10th, 2026

Genuine governance. ON the surface, the Punjab cabinet’s decision to allocate funds for local government elections is a welcome step towards restoring a democratic tier of governance that has remained absent for more than four years — in fact, for much longer in practical terms. After years of premature dissolution, court-mandated reinstatement, repeated delays and legal and administrative manoeuvring, the allocation suggests that Punjab is finally preparing to hold polls that were constitutionally due by April 2022 . The timing, however, is difficult to ignore. The announcement comes only days after the interior minister , with the public endorsement of DG ISPR , argued that creating new provinces or administrative units could improve governance. The sudden will to revive LGs may well be aimed at demonstrating that devolution to the grassroots can improve governance and that LGs offer an alternative to redrawing provincial boundaries as proposed by certain quarters. That argument would have carried weight had Punjab chosen to establish a genuinely empowered LG system. Unfortunately, it has done the opposite. The existing Punjab LG law is devolution only in name. While it provides for elected councils, it concentrates meaningful administrative and financial authority in the hands of the provincial government and bureaucracy, making elected local representatives dependent on the goodwill of officials for even routine decisions. Such an arrangement defeats the very purpose of LGs, which is to bring decision-making closer to the citizens. Punjab’s legislation compares unfavourably even with that of other provinces where LGs enjoy relatively greater governance space. The country’s largest province has opted for perhaps the most centralised model of local governance. The experience of the past six decades illustrates why merely holding elections is not enough. Successive governments have dissolved local bodies and amended or replaced LG laws at their whim. Thus a constitutional obligation has been repeatedly ignored and grassroots democracy treated as an optional exercise rather than a permanent feature of governance. Meaningful devolution requires much more than elected councillors. A truly functional third tier of government must have constitutionally protected administrative and financial autonomy. LGs should be able to raise, allocate and spend resources without provincial interference. The local bureaucracy and police should be accountable to elected local representatives rather than exclusively to the province. Without such authority, elected councils are little more than advisory bodies with limited capacity to address citizens’ issues. The governance challenges of Punjab — and of other provinces — stem from the excessive centralisation of power. Holding polls under a law that denies genuine autonomy to LGs may satisfy a constitutional formality. But it will not resolve the governance deficit that has fuelled demands for more provinces to improve governance. Published in Dawn, August 10th, 2026

High court judge to investigate Mir Raza murder case, says home minister. • Announcement comes hours after Faryal Talpur recommends judicial probe • Previous investigation body sent packing as IGP forms new team • DSP, Jauhar SHO suspended for failing to preserve crime scene • Sharjeel moves NCCIA over ‘defamatory campaign’ KARACHI: In what appears to be a damage-control exercise, the provincial government has decided to conduct a judicial inquiry by a judge of the Sindh High Court into the murder of young businessman Mir Raza Ali, a day after a fresh autopsy ruled out the possibility of suicide on the grounds that he had been shot in the back and that his body bore marks of torture. An announcement to this effect was made by Sindh Home Minister Zia Lanjar a few hours after senior Pakistan Peoples Party leader and chairperson of the Sindh Assembly’s Standing Committee on Home Affairs, Faryal Talpur, recommended that the chief minister constitute a judicial commission to conduct a transparent, impartial and comprehensive investigation into the case. An IBA graduate and owner of the eatery Wafflix, Mir Raza had gone missing on July 28, and his body was found a day later with a gunshot wound in bushes near Shahi Qila Ground in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. When investigators reportedly focused their probe on the possibility of suicide and reports emerged about a flawed autopsy, Raza’s family filed an application before a judicial magistrate seeking the exhumation of the body for a fresh post-mortem examination. While the magistrate ordered the exhumation, the provincial government changed the composition of the medical board three times, fuelling rumours that there was an attempt to cover up the case. Later, the government restored the original medical board that had carried out the exhumation and conducted the autopsy and found that he had suffered injuries and had been shot in the back. On Sunday, in an attempt to show the public that there’s nothing to hide, senior PPP leader Faryal Talpur recommended a judicial commission, saying it should examine all aspects of the incident and bring the facts to light. “Legal and disciplinary action should be taken without discrimination against those found responsible in light of the commission’s findings,” she added. Talpur stressed that justice for the victim’s family must be ensured at all costs and that the public should be transparently informed of all facts surrounding the case. “No negligence or bias will be tolerated in meeting the requirements of justice,” she said, adding that providing justice to the bereaved family and maintaining public confidence in the justice system were fundamental responsibilities of the government and relevant institutions. A few hours after Talpur’s statement, Home Minister Lanjar and Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab reached deceased Raza’s residence, met with his father, Mir Hussain Ali, and assured the family that they would be provided complete justice. Talking to the media after the meeting, Lanjar said a decision had been taken to conduct a judicial inquiry, under the supervision of a Sindh High Court judge, into the murder case. He said a transparent and impartial investigation would be ensured. Speaking on the occasion, Mayor Wahab noted that Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah chaired a four-hour-long meeting during which “all aspects of the incident and the investigation were reviewed in detail”. New investigation team formed The Sindh police chief dismissed the previous investigation team headed by Special Investigation Unit SSP Dr Samiullah Soomro and appointed DIG Amir Farooqi to lead a five-member new committee. Other members of the committee are SSP Syed Muhammad Ali Raza, SP Qais Khan, SP Anam Tajjamul and Inspector Ch. Ghazanfar. According to a notification, “The team shall undertake a comprehensive and impartial investigation into the case from all relevant angles. The team shall identify, collect, preserve and examine any new or additional evidence and shall thoroughly examine and analyse all physical, technical, circumstantial and forensic evidence collected during the investigation. “The team shall make all-out efforts to work out the case and submit a report to the court concerned within the stipulated period. The team may co-opt any officer to assist in the investigation. Progress shall be reported on a day-to-day basis,” it added. DSP, Jauhar SHO suspended Karachi police chief Azad Khan has suspended Sharea Faisal DSP Muhammad Arshad Afridi and Gulistan-i-Jauhar SHO Kamran Qureshi with immediate effect. A police spokesperson said that both officials were suspended for failing to preserve the crime scene and conduct a proper crime-scene investigation after the body of Mir Raza was found. Sharjeel moves NCCIA against ‘malicious social media campaign’ Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon, through his counsel, filed an application before the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) against unknown persons for “causing harassment, creating false and malicious content on social media against him and his son. The application stated that certain social media accounts began circulating posts, videos and statements against Memon and his son, containing “allegations that are false, baseless, fabricated, and malicious in nature, and which are calculated to injure their reputation, dignity, and standing in society”. Memon stated that none of the allegations — that he owned the guest house in Gulistan-i-Jauhar, where Mir Raza was allegedly tortured and murdered and that his son had left for London immediately after the incident and has since been moving around with a bodyguard — has “any factual or evidentiary basis, and each is false, baseless, and malicious, being designed solely to malign” him and his son for extraneous political motives. His lawyer asked the NCCIA to register an FIR and proceed in accordance with law against the persons found responsible under the applicable provisions of the Prevention of Electronic Crime Act 2016 and any other law found attracted. Judicial probe launched into death of 2 girls in Lahore police custody. LAHORE: A judicial magistrate has initiated an inquiry under Section 176 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) into the suspicious death of two underage girls in Lahore police custody on Aug 4, as mystery continues to surround the horrific, tragic incident. The judicial inquiry was launched after the families of the victims – Amina and Anmol – demanded an impartial investigation into what happened to the girls in the police custody for well over two hours – from the time of their arrest to calling a Rescue 1122 team to the Township police station on Aug 4. Section 176 of the CrPC empowers a magistrate to inquire into the cause of death when a person dies in police custody or under some suspicious circumstances. The law also empowers the magistrate to order exhumation of a body for the postmortem examination, besides recording statements and examining witnesses on oath. Dawn spoke to police officers familiar with the matter and attempted to map the sequence of events from the girls’ arrest to their deaths. According to an official, around 2:54pm on Aug 4 an emergency call was received on police helpline 15 from complainant, Zeshan Latif, who alleged that two girls entered his house and fraudulently stole gold jewellery and cash belonging to his wife. A sub-inspector (SI) of the Township police, Ghulam Ghous, reached the scene at 3:11pm and brought the two girls to the police station, where they were handed over to the duty clerk (Muharrar), Tasnim Arif, at 3:26pm. Mr Latif subsequently submitted an application, which was e-tagged at 4:40pm, and an FIR was registered at 4:50pm against the two girls. The Township police station then recorded a report at 5:20pm regarding the transfer of the girls’ custody from the operations wing to the investigation staff. According to the official, the operations wing’s muharrar claimed that, following registration of the FIR, he handed over the girls to the investigation wing Muharrar Bilal, in accordance with the prescribed procedure. The situation took a grim turn shortly afterwards when, at 6:03pm, the central office of Rescue 1122 received an emergency call from the Township police regarding the deteriorating condition of both girls. A Rescue 1122 team reached the police station at 6:14pm and found one of the girls “almost dead”, while the other was unconscious, according to the official. Both were shifted to Jinnah Hospital, where doctors pronounced the unconscious girl dead. The other girl, who was reportedly in critical condition, also died shortly after in the hospital. As news of the girls’ death spread, senior police officers from the Saddar Division’s operations and investigation wings reached the Township police station at around 9:30pm and sensing gravity of the situation apprised higher authorities about the incident. The official says that incident triggered a row between the operations and investigation wings, with officers from both sides reportedly shifting the responsibility for the girls’ custody onto each other. The time between 3:11pm, when the girls were taken into custody, and 6:03pm, when Rescue 1122 was called, is therefore crucial in the judicial inquiry, he adds. Video footage that surfaced after the incident shows the girls apparently in a relatively stable condition when they were brought to the police station. In one recording, a police official can be seen questioning them. Another video recorded by a camera installed in the duty clerk’s room shows Amina and Anmol sitting on chairs inside the police station. They appear conscious and are seen interacting with the duty clerk before leaving the room. Police officials, however, say that details of the girls’ interaction and interrogation are not covered by the station’s security cameras. Immediately after the incident, the investigation police claimed that drug overdose was the likely cause of the girls’ death. The claim, however, has yet to be conclusively established through the postmortem reports, which are crucial evidence in determining the death cause. Police were still awaiting the final postmortem reports when Dawn spoke to officials. Investigation SSP Mohammad Naveed strongly rejected allegations that the girls had been tortured in custody. “Though I am not aware whether the final postmortem reports have been issued, I can assure you that the allegations of custodial torture are absolutely false and misleading,” he claimed. The SSP alleges that both girls were chronic drug users and had apparently consumed a strong addictive substance before being brought to the police station. “During their custody at the police station, they fainted, probably because of the impact of the drugs they had consumed, and later died of the same cause,” he claimed. Mr Naveed maintains that as a major portion of the girls interrogation had been captured by surveillance cameras installed at the police station, it shows girls were not maltreated in custody. He says the judicial inquiry had been initiated at the request of senior police officers under Section 176 of the CrPC and that its findings would bring out the circumstances of the deaths. Asked why the case had not been referred to the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), the SSP said the agency is usually asked to investigate the cases involving allegations that a suspect had died as a result of custodial torture or killed in a police encounter. “This case is different, as it concerns the deaths of two suspects in custody, and there was no need for an FIA investigation,” he insisted. The judicial inquiry is expected to examine the circumstances surrounding the girls’ detention, the transfer of their custody between the operations and investigation wings, the available CCTV footage, statements of police officials and witnesses, and the postmortem reports’ findings to dig out the facts. Prime suspect in Rs8.5bn Yellow Line graft case under NAB scrutiny. KARACHI: The legal troubles of the prime suspect in the Rs8.5 billion Yellow Line graft case, Zameer Abbasi, have further increased as the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) has initiated an inquiry into his alleged possession of assets beyond his known sources of income and his alleged “illegal appointments” or “promotions in the Sindh government”. Earlier in June, the Anti-Corruption Establishment (ACE) Sindh had booked Abbasi, the then project director of the Karachi Mobility Project (KMP), and others following an inquiry into alleged financial mismanagement in the KMP related to the Yellow Line. The inquiry committee report stated that Abbasi and then director procurement Jhaman made Rs8.5bn advance payments to contractors without bank guarantees despite the fact that their contracts lacked any specific clause regarding “advance payment and financial assistance to the contractors”. A source told Dawn that the NAB had initiated an inquiry against the senior bureaucrat over allegations of possessing assets beyond his known sources of income and illegal appointments or promotions in the Sindh government. Bureau seeks details of Zameer Abbasi’s assets, ‘illegal’ appointments, promotions As part of the inquiry, the bureau has sought details of immovable properties registered in the names of Abbasi, his wife and children and other family members from the concerned departments. According to the source, Abbasi began his career with NAB and was later deputed to the Sindh police as a DSP. After a Supreme Court directive, he was repatriated to his parent department, the NAB, where he served until 2016. In the same year, he was appointed as a grade-17 section officer. The appointment was challenged before a court on allegations that it was made through irregularities and that he had also received an out-of-turn promotion, the source claimed. The source further alleged that Abbasi had also approached the court, contending that his colleagues who had joined service with him had already been promoted to grade 19. However, before the court could decide his petition, he was promoted to grade 19, the source claimed. In 2022, he was appointed to another key position, but the appointment was challenged before a court, which suspended the notification. Although he subsequently disappeared from the public spotlight for some time, he was later appointed to another important position, the source added. The ACE only managed to apprehend Abbasi, a grade-19 officer of the Sindh government, claiming that he was arrested in Lahore and later produced him before the court concerned in Karachi. The provincial anti-corruption court also rejected his post-arrest bail application. Published in Dawn, August 10th, 2026

Mir Raza’s grave is not a silent one. There is a particular cruelty in a name being spoken twice by death. Once when it is buried. And once when it is dug up again, because the truth could not rest with it. Mir Raza, the son of Mir Hassan Ali Khan, and Wafflix business owner, was laid into the earth of Rehorania Masjid graveyard on the 29th of July. Eleven days later, a board of doctors, a police surgeon, a magistrate, and a family that refused to let silence be the final word stood over that same soil and opened it again. I have read the report. I do not think I will ever be able to unread it. It is written in the flat, careful language that medicine keeps for what it cannot otherwise bear to say. Somewhere inside that distance is a twenty-five-year-old man who once had a face his mother could recognise without being told his name. What the doctors found confirmed what the family had feared all along, that Mir Raza did not simply die. He was taken from them. And when asked, plainly, whether his wounds came before death, someone circled a single word on the page: Yes . That word has not left me since. What stays with me most is not the injury itself, but the effort that surrounded it. The care taken. The insistence, even now, that this body still deserved to be handled gently, named properly, treated as someone rather than something. Dr Summaiya Syed, Police Surgeon of Karachi, stood at that graveside and did what very few of us are ever asked to do. She looked directly at what injustice leaves behind, and she did not turn away. There is a particular kind of courage in choosing, on an ordinary working day, to be the last honest witness a murdered man will ever have. It is not the courage of headlines. It is quieter than that, and heavier, and it asks everything of the stomach and the soul, and gives back only the satisfaction of having told the truth when it would have been so much easier not to. And yet, the final word on how Mir Raza died has still not been given. Not because there is doubt. The findings speak clearly enough. It has simply not been said out loud, in the way that matters, in the place that matters. Twelve days passed, the doctors believe, between his death and the moment anyone was able to examine him. Twelve days in which a family did not know. And then more days still, in which even his grave had to be argued for, before the truth was allowed to be looked at a second time. We spend our lives pretending we are not what that grave revealed. We make plans, we argue over small things, we behave as though we will always have tomorrow to fix what we said today. But strip away the years, and every one of us ends the same way Mir Raza did. Plain. Unrecognisable, even to those who loved us most. If that is where we are all headed, then what exactly are we fighting for when we fight for justice? I do not think it is the body. The earth takes that regardless. I think it is the truth of what was done to someone while they were still here to feel it. That is the only part of us that does not decay. It is the only inheritance a murdered man can leave behind that no grave is deep enough to bury. Karachi did not let this one go quiet. Somewhere between a graveyard and a courtroom, ordinary people, neighbours, strangers, a city that has buried too many of its sons without asking enough questions, decided that Mir Raza’s silence was not going to be mistaken for peace. They spoke. They kept speaking, until an order was signed and a grave that should have been the end of his story became instead the place where it finally began to be told properly. That is not a small thing. In a country where so many cases are allowed to fade as quietly as a body returns to the earth, the refusal of ordinary citizens to look away is very often the only justice the dead will ever be given. So I find myself asking the only question I have left. If the truth has already been found, plainly, and written down, and confirmed by a circled word on a page, then what are we still waiting for? Where does justice go, in the space between a death and its acknowledgment? And where, in a city that loved this man loudly enough to bring him back up into the light so his story could be told rightly, does our humanity actually stand today? Not in the vigils. Not in the slogans. But in the quiet, unglamorous work of finishing what we started for Mir Raza. I do not have that answer yet. I am not sure any of us do. But I know this much. A city that will not let its dead be forgotten has not yet forgotten itself. And whatever else remains unresolved, that much still holds true: somewhere beneath all our exhaustion and all our grief, we still believe a man’s name is worth saying twice. Malaysian PM Anwar Ibrahim undergoing medical procedures, aide says. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is undergoing medical tests and procedures and was expected to be under observation for two days, his aide said on Monday. Anwar is “undergoing examinations and procedures set by a team of medical experts”, Press Secretary Tunku Nashrul Abaidah said in a statement, without providing further details. “Let us pray … that he is blessed with long-lasting health so that he can return to his usual duties in the near future,” the statement said. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif wished his Malaysian counterpart a speedy recovery. In a post on X, he said: “Wishing my dear brother, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, a swift and smooth recovery during his medical procedures.” “The people of Pakistan join me in praying for his continued good health and well-being,” he added. Anwar, who turned 79 on Monday and has been in office since 2022, has had recurrent shoulder and back problems. He was hospitalised in 2018 for shoulder and back pain. Last November, he cancelled a trip to Pahang state due to back pain. In January, he was issued a clean bill of health after undergoing a routine medical examination, according to a hospital statement.

Kuwait felicitates Pakistan on Makkah defence deal. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar received a phone call from Kuwait’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, wherein the latter felicitated the former on the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Monday. According to the FO, the two dignitaries spoke late on Sunday and also “exchanged views on the regional situation, including occupied East Jerusalem”. They also discussed bilateral relations between the two countries and “matters of mutual interest, including the follow-up to FM Jarrah’s recent visit to Pakistan and further enhancing cooperation and investment in key sectors”. “The two sides agreed to remain closely engaged,” the FO added. Earlier, DPM Dar had also spoken to Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand. “The two exchanged views on the regional situation, including the recently signed Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye,” the FO said. It added that Dar shared the “essence of the agreement” and the “joint resolve of the three countries to contribute to regional peace, stability and security”. The joint defence agreement, signed in Makkah on Friday, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empowers its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. On Sunday, Dar said that the agreement remained “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles after the Turkish foreign minister said Egypt could be joining the pact. “The Makkah accord is the culmination of years of discussions and coordination, with a common desire to strengthen strategic cooperation in addressing multifarious peace and security challenges and advancing regional peace, stability and prosperity,” Dar said. He clarified that the pact did not abrogate or replace any existing bilateral or multilateral agreements between the signatory countries, or with other countries or organisations. Reiterating that any external armed attack on any one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all under the pact, he said it was consistent with the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Moreover, he said, the accord was “purely defensive” in nature. “It is not targeted against any country and its sole purpose is to further strengthen our ongoing efforts towards peace, stability and prosperity in the wider region.” “The Makkah Accord remains open to any country in the region willing to uphold its fundamental principles and resolve differences through mutual respect, cooperation and peaceful means,” he said, adding that the pact was consistent with the fundamental pillars of Islamabad’s foreign policy. “Pakistan looks forward to continuing to work closely with all brotherly countries in the region towards lasting peace and stability. We remain committed to advancing the cause of peaceful resolution of all conflicts and building a more secure, stable and prosperous future for our peoples,” he concluded.

3rd phase of AJK polls: Voting underway in Poonch Division's Bagh and Haveli districts. The third phase of elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) is currently underway in four constituencies in Poonch Division’s Bagh and Haveli districts. Polling began at 8am and will continue until 5pm. Government officials have anticipated clashes in some areas, while the Election Commission has classified most of the 803 polling stations in the four constituencies as either sensitive or highly sensitive. “Apart from the regular police of both districts, we have dispatched an additional 10,300 troops to maintain law and order and provide a fear-free atmosphere to voters,” Election Commission Secretary Raja Mohammad Shakeel told Dawn earlier. Elections are being held across AJK in phases amid tensions between protesters and the authorities. Polling in Mirpur and Muzaff­arabad divisions was held on July 27 and Aug 2, respectively, with the PML-N securing 24 seats. The PPP has only secured 10 seats so far. The third phase of the polls was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division. The division comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, last week the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli due to concerns over the law and order situation. The AJK election commissioner has hinted that polling on the remaining seven constituencies could be held by Aug 20 or 21. Malpractice, rigging allegations Polling in previous phases of the elections was marred by allegations of rigging, scuffles and violence, with the PPP and the PML-N — the main contenders in AJK but allies in the Centre — engaging in a war of words. The PPP has accused the PML-N of rigging and electoral malpractices in the previous phases. It continued to allege rigging in Haveli and Bagh as well. In a series of posts on X, the PPP shared complaints it said it had filed to the Election Commission. In one of the complaints, the PPP alleged that roads leading to the Banni Marasira area had been blocked, where PML-N supporters were illegally stamping ballot papers at 12 polling stations in the LA-15 constituency. “The commission is requested to consider the two acts together rather than separately, because the second is made possible by the first,” the party said, adding that officials, voters, polling agents and party workers were unable to reach the polling stations “to see what is being done inside”. The party also claimed delays in polling at LA-15’s polling station no.87 in Thub. It also alleged that polling at stations no.143 and 144 in Hatala Pader did not commence on time due to the non-arrival of polling staff. The PPP also alleged that its polling agent was “forcibly removed” from LA-15’s station no.158 in Makhdoom Kot. Rathore, two ex-AJK PMs face crucial electoral test Meanwhile, AJK Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore, who is from the PPP, and two of his predecessors — Sardar Tanveer Ilyas and Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan — face a battle for political survival as voters head to the polls. Around 238,664 men and 221,707 women are eligible to cast their ballots at 803 polling stations comprising 1,254 polling booths. A total of 82 candidates are in the fray, with LA-14 (Dhirkot) attracting the highest number of candidates at 30 and LA-17 (Haveli) the lowest at nine. In LA-17, Rathore is facing PML-N candidate Engr Mohsin Aziz and independent candidate Khawaja Tariq Saeed, a member of the AJK Council. Rathore and Saeed had been political allies and, under an agreement, had agreed to contest the seat alternately. However, after becoming prime minister, Rathore asked Saeed to step aside in his favour, a request he did not accept, turning the former allies into rivals. Aziz, whose father, Chaudhry Mohammad Aziz, had won the seat at least three times, draws support from the sizeable Gujjar community. Saeed, meanwhile, is believed to enjoy the backing of a sizeable section of the Kashmiri community, as well as an alliance of several smaller clans. Rathore, however, remains confident of retaining the seat, citing the performance of his government during his relatively brief tenure as prime minister. In LA-15 (Wasti Bagh), former prime minister Ilyas is facing PML-N candidate and former minister Mushtaq Ahmed Minhas, PPP nominee and sitting minister Sardar Ziaul Qamar, and Jamaat-i-Islami candidate retired Brig Dr Mohammad Khan, a respected educationist. Ilyas, who secured a little over 3,300 votes from Upper Neelum in the second phase of the elections, had initially announced a boycott of the third phase. He subsequently reversed the decision and resumed campaigning, claiming that his victory would enable the constituency to “secure either the presidency or prime ministership.” Ilyas and Qamar belong to the same Madiyal tribe, while Brig Khan belongs to the Narma clan and enjoys the support of former JI chief Abdul Rashid Turabi and former adviser Raja Yasin Khan. Minhas has the advantage of belonging to the PML-N, which is poised to form the next government after emerging as the largest party in the elections held so far. His campaign has also stressed the argument that voters should elect a candidate from the party that is set to occupy the government benches rather than send their representative to the opposition. In LA-16 (Sharqi Bagh), former ministers Sardar Mir Akbar and Sardar Qamar Zaman are the principal contenders, representing the PML-N and PPP, respectively. The fourth contest, LA-14 (Dhirkot), has drawn particular attention because of the challenge faced by Sardar Attique, head of the once-dominant Muslim Conference (MC). Attique is reportedly facing a strong challenge from Sajid Iqbal Abbasi of the relatively new Awam Dast-o-Bazu Party. A contractor and philanthropist, Abbasi is said to have spent millions of rupees from his own resources on public welfare projects in the constituency, helping him build a sizeable personal following. Attique, who has represented the constituency successively since 2006, when he first became prime minister, faces an additional challenge in that Abbasi also belongs to the same tribe. Among nearly two dozen other candidates are PML-N’s nominee Raja Faisal Azad and PPP candidate Raja Mubashar Ejaz. Security forces kill 5 terrorists in intelligence-based operation in Balochistan's Panjgur. The operation was conducted as part of Operation Radd-ul-Fitna-3 in Balochistan, the state broadcaster said. “According to security sources, the security forces conducted an intelligence-based operation against Fitna al Hindustan terrorists in Sarkani and Chedgi areas of Panjgur, killing five terrorists, including a key Fitna al Hindustan commander, Wazir,” it said. The terrorists were allegedly involved in robbery, extortion, kidnapping and attacks targeting local traders and other residents in Panjgur, it added. Paying tribute to the professionalism and operational capabilities of the security forces, Naqvi said the successful action had thwarted the nefarious designs of the terrorists and dealt a major blow to their activities in the region. Naqvi said the successful operation demonstrated the security forces’ preparedness, professionalism and unwavering commitment to combating terrorism. He stressed that the elimination of terrorist elements was essential for restoring lasting peace and stability in Balochistan and across the country. He said the government and the people remained committed to supporting the security forces in their efforts to eradicate terrorist networks and ensure peace and security throughout the country. The operation comes a day after security forces killed 15 terrorists in multiple intelligence-based operations across Balochistan. The operations were conducted in Mastung, Bolan, Washuk, Awaran, Sibi, Khuzdar, Harnai and Nushki under Operation Radd-ul-Fitna-3, according to state media. The latest operations by the security forces in Balochistan take place as the province continues to face security challenges. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies’ (PICSS) monthly security assessment released on July 31, the security situation deteriorated most significantly in Balochistan in the country last month. The overall death toll increased by 241pc in Balochistan, from 109 in June to 372 in July, the report said. Security personnel deaths in Balochistan increased from six in June to 62 in July, representing a rise of 933pc. Terrorist deaths rose from 75 to 238, while civilian deaths increased by 93pc, from 28 to 54. Eighteen members of peace committees were also killed in the province. Last month, security forces and law enforcement personnel jointly launched Operation Shaban in Balochistan in retaliation for a deadly attack on a police post at the Mangi Dam pumping station in Ziarat on July 6 when armed attackers kidnapped and killed 27 police officers .

'Work is work, it has to be done': Brickmakers in Pakistan scorched by sun above and fire below. As dark plumes billow from overhead smokestacks, brickmakers at a kiln in Sheikhupura district crush coal through small holes beneath their feet into the fiery chambers below. Workers already have to endure extreme conditions at traditional brick kilns, which burn at over 1,000°C and demand constant monitoring to ensure they remain hot enough. But they are becoming almost unbearable as climate change makes summers even hotter in a country already used to temperatures well over 40°C . A man works at a brick kiln in Sheikhupura, Punjab on July 20, 2026. —AFP Abid Hussain, a 35-year-old labourer whose clothes were covered in dark soot, told AFP the work felt like being trapped between fire below and, increasingly, above. He is one of hundreds of thousands working in an industry that labour advocates say is poorly regulated, badly paid and becoming more dangerous as temperatures rise. “The heat is undoubtedly extreme but when you think about the financial pressures at home, you have no option but to keep working,” Hussain said. Fast-growing Pakistan’s construction boom is increasing the demand for labour in the sector, in which workers earn around $3 a day. Despite the scorching sun and dust filling the air, workers stay on the heated kiln surface for hours at a time. “I would describe these brick kilns as places of confinement,” said Syeda Ghulam Fatima, the General Secretary of the Bonded Labour Liberation Front Pakistan. “Workers endure relentless heat from the blazing sun overhead while the intense heat radiating from the kiln rises beneath them.” The workers remain trapped in a cycle of debt, extreme heat, and deteriorating health, Fatima told AFP, adding rising global temperatures amplified the risks. Nationwide, more than 18,000 brick kilns employ a total of over a million people, according to 2018 data in a Climate and Clean Air Coalition report. A man works at a brick kiln in Sheikhupura, Punjab on July 20, 2026. —AFP Pakistan is ranked among the countries most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change globally, according to experts. Fatima said many workers receive advance payments, making them unable to decline to work in dangerous conditions without falling into burdensome debt. Hussain, who earns roughly 25,000 rupees a month, said the money barely covers rent and his children’s basic needs. “No matter the situation, whether we are ill or there are family matters, we still have to work,” he said. “If I take time off, we’ll be in trouble.” Breaks ‘not possible’ There is some hope of improved conditions from the Punjab provincial government’s push to convert the industry to more modern technology known as zigzag kilns, which reduce air pollution and respiratory hazards. Health experts warn that, especially at traditional kilns, prolonged heat exposure makes brick workers more vulnerable to illnesses including skin disorders, respiratory problems, and kidney disease. An aerial view shows a brick kiln in Sheikhupura, in Punjab on July 20, 2026. —AFP But “extended rest breaks are not feasible… whether it is extreme heat, cold, or rain, the work must continue uninterrupted”, said Mujeeb Ullah, 45, the supervisor at the kiln, adding its temperatures needed to be kept stable. He said they provided workers with drinking water and occasional short breaks. On the other side of the compound, a man squatted next to rows of unbaked bricks, mixing wet mud and packing it by hand into a wooden mould — exhausting work considering the temperatures. A man works at a brick kiln in Sheikhupura, Punjab on July 20, 2026. —AFP Worker Muhammad Azeem, 28, said there was no alternative. “As for the weather, whether it is good or bad, work is work, it has to be done.”
