Malabon DRRMO warns residents as La Mesa Dam nears spilling level. The Malabon City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (DRRMO) warned residents on Monday, Aug. 10, to remain alert and prepare for possible evacuation as the water level at La Mesa Dam neared its spilling level. As of 10 a.m., the city government said the dam’s water level had reached 80.05 meters, just 0.10 meter below its 80.15-meter spilling level. It added that the water level of the Tullahan River was recorded at 12 meters, nearing its 12.5-meter spilling level. The Malabon DRRMO advised residents to prepare emergency go-bags, move belongings to higher areas, and be ready to evacuate once instructed by the city government or barangay officials. Authorities also urged residents to remain vigilant as the city continues to monitor La Mesa Dam and the Tullahan River amid persistent rains. Meanwhile, at least 24 families have already evacuated due to flooding in several parts of the city. The city government said 16 families are staying at Tinajeros Elementary School, five at Maysilo Elementary School, and three at Panghulo Elementary School. As of 8 a.m., flooding was reported in 15 areas, although all monitored roads remained passable to all types of vehicles. Floodwaters reached gutter level, or around six inches, in Sitio 6 in Barangay Catmon, Burgos in Barangay Concepcion, Don Basilio in Barangay Hulong Duhat, M.H. Del Pilar in Barangay Maysilo, and Silver Swan in Barangay Panghulo. Flooding ranging from one to six inches was also recorded in parts of Dampalit, Ibaba, San Agustin, Santulan, and Tañong. No flooding was monitored in Acacia, Baritan, Bayan-Bayanan, Flores, Longos, Muzon, Niugan, Potrero, Tinajeros, Tonsuya, Tugatog, and several other areas as of 8 a.m. The city government said monitoring of flood conditions and water levels is ongoing.

Marcos orders expanded relief efforts as gov’t logs 12 deaths from ‘Luis,’ ‘Maymay,’ habagat. President Marcos has ordered government agencies to ensure that assistance reaches all residents affected by Tropical Storm Luis, Typhoon Maymay, and the southwest monsoon, or habagat, as the government recorded 12 casualties from the combined weather disturbances. Marcos convened a situation briefing at Malacañang with Cabinet officials on Monday, Aug. 10, to assess the impact of the weather systems and direct immediate response and relief operations in affected areas. In a press briefing, Presidential Communications Office Undersecretary Claire Castro said Marcos specifically directed agencies to reach affected residents in remote areas and ensure that assistance also reaches those who had already returned home from evacuation centers. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), together with local governments, has provided P39.37 million in assistance to affected residents in several regions. The assistance has reached communities in Metro Manila, Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Cordillera Administrative Region, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, Bicol Region, Western Visayas, and Zamboanga Peninsula. Thousands deployed Castro said in her press briefing that the government has deployed 3,841 personnel for possible search-and-rescue operations, while another 4,392 personnel and 943 pieces of equipment remain on standby for immediate deployment if needed. Fourteen air assets and one naval asset from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), Philippine National Police (PNP), and Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) have also been deployed, with additional resources from the Office of Civil Defense (OCD), Philippine Navy, and Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) on standby. The DSWD has distributed 54,370 family food packs, 2,722 ready-to-eat food items, 23 other food items, and 1,376 non-food items, while nearly P1 million in financial assistance has been released under its Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation program. Nationwide, the agency has nearly five million family food packs and 245,474 non-food items ready for distribution, along with P1.61 billion in standby funds. Flood-control work continues Marcos also ordered the continued implementation of measures to reduce the impact of flooding, including sustained work in areas affected by the recent rains. Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vince Dizon earlier inspected flood-control initiatives in Las Piñas, while the agency continued dredging operations, installation of high-density polyethylene pipes, and operation of pumping stations to prevent rivers and waterways from overflowing. Castro said Marcos also called on local governments and residents to work together in addressing flooding, including through proper waste disposal, as part of a whole-of-nation approach.

Western Europe sets new temperature record as heat waves pummel the region. BERLIN (AP) — The heat waves roiling Western Europe this summer toppled an average temperature record for the June-July period set in 2022, according to the European climate agency Copernicus. The extreme heat began in May and has contributed to major wildfires , prolonged drought and new national temperature records across the region, as well as thousands of projected heat-related deaths. Globally , so far this is the third-hottest year, behind 2024 and 2025, climate statistics show. But 2026 still has time to catch up. Thanks to the one-two punch of accelerated human-caused global warming and a supersized El Niño , a periodic warming of parts of the Pacific that leads to temperature variations around the globe, there’s an increasing chance that by the end of the year, 2026 could become the hottest year on record, beating out 2024 — or at least come close, scientists said. Last month saw the highest average sea surface temperature ever recorded for July across the extra-polar oceans, or the oceans free of seasonal sea ice, Copernicus said. That was partially fueled by developing El Niño conditions in the equatorial Pacific, the service said. The new average record for July is 20.96 degrees Celsius (69.73 degrees Fahrenheit), which beat the 2023 record of 20.89 C (69.60 F). But last month’s average surface air temperature globally was 16.90°C (62.42 F), making it only the joint second warmest July on record and tied with July 2024, Copernicus reported. In Western Europe, meanwhile, the average temperature record for the June-July period hit 21.62°C (70.92 F), Copernicus said. “Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over western Europe, the extreme temperatures also amplified widespread drought. As soils dry out, they lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing heat to build more readily,” said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. "This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another.”

Margarita Penson brings vibrant abstraction to Melbourne. Margarita Patrice Sy Penson is equally at home in two very different worlds. As a supply chain professional, she works with the structured digital data of goods and logistics. As an abstract expressionist artist, she turns to bold brushstrokes, kinetic movement and vibrant colors to translate raw emotions and fleeting experiences onto canvas. That artistic practice is currently being presented in Melbourne, Australia, where six of Margarita's acrylic compositions are part of an exhibition and art fair at Quadrant Gallery alongside five fellow artists. During the weekend of Aug. 22, Penson's body of work will become the gallery's main feature. Among the works on display are "Ekpyrosis" and "'Chak Phra Afternoon," two paintings marked by textured layers of red, rust and burnt umber. Their warm, luminous tones give the compositions a sense of movement and intensity. "Chak Phra Afternoon" has a particularly personal origin. According to Margarita , the painting was sparked by an involuntary rush of sensory recall while she was in a Bangkok restaurant during an exhilarating festival. "I aim to capture and connect a tempo of feelings and fleeting mundane sentiments with viewers," She says of her work. Her palette shifts in other works, moving from the fiery reds and orange glows into cooler grays and blues. Using both brush and palette knife, Margarita creates compositions that move into open areas of white, producing a calmer mood that invites viewers toward quiet reflection. A freewheeling traveler, Margarita is based in Manila and comes from an artistic family. She is the granddaughter of writer and painter Maria Lourdes de Vera, one of the country's few exponents of surrealism. Her Melbourne presentation features works completed in 2026, including "Flow I," a 70-by-50-centimeter acrylic on canvas; "Ekpyrosis," measuring 50 by 60 centimeters; and "Chak Phra Afternoon," also measuring 50 by 60 centimeters. The three works offer different expressions of Penson's use of color, texture and movement. Margarita's artistic activities continue when she returns to the Philippines. From Aug. 25-28, she will participate in the back-to-back exhibition "Pamana at Sining ng Pamantasan sa Gunita nina Amorsolo at Manansala" at the UP Manila Museum of a History of Ideas. For an artist working between the precision of a supply chain career and the freedom of abstract expressionism, Margarita 's current exhibitions offer a look at how different experiences can find their way onto canvas. In Melbourne, six works bring her energetic compositions to a wider audience, while her upcoming Manila exhibition will offer local viewers another opportunity to encounter her developing body of work.

315 rising Filipino songwriters take center stage at FILSCAP's biggest 'Songwriters' Night Select'. The future of Original Pilipino Music (OPM) took center stage as the Filipino Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers (FILSCAP) celebrated Linggo ng Musikang Pilipino with its biggest Songwriters' Night Select yet. Held on July 31 at the Music Museum, the annual concert attracted more than 1,000 registrants, making it the largest edition of the event to date. More than a concert, Songwriters' Night Select has become FILSCAP's flagship platform for discovering, developing, and celebrating the country's next generation of songwriters. This year's event brought together music lovers, industry partners, and supporters to witness 15 emerging songwriters from Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao perform their original compositions on one of the country's premier concert stages. FILSCAP Chairman Ramon Chuaying shared that “Music has always been a powerful way of bringing people together,” and that this year’s FILSCAP Songwriters’ Night Select was a reminder of the stories, cultures, and experiences that shape Filipino artistry. He added that OPM continues to grow through the creativity and unique perspectives of today’s artists, with FILSCAP remaining committed to celebrating regional diversity and nurturing individual artistry. The evening formally opened with inspiring remarks from Jim Paredes, who reflected on the remarkable journey of this year's performers. He shared that the 15 featured songwriters were carefully selected from more than 300 aspiring composers who joined FILSCAP's nationwide Songwriters' Night Open Mic Series. Representing different regions of the country, the finalists showcased the richness, diversity, and promise of Filipino songwriting. Paredes emphasized that Songwriters' Night Select is one of FILSCAP's most important initiatives in championing original Filipino music by giving emerging creators the opportunity to be heard, recognized, and celebrated. That support extended well beyond the concert stage. From the time the finalists were selected, FILSCAP provided the resources and assistance needed to help them prepare for the event, allowing them to focus on their performances and their music. The initiative reflects the organization's continued commitment to supporting Filipino songwriters by creating opportunities for emerging creators to develop their craft and share their work with a wider audience. The celebration was made even more meaningful by the presence of FILSCAP's Board of Trustees, whose vision and initiative continue to guide the growth of Songwriters' Night Select. Their commitment to expanding the program has strengthened FILSCAP's efforts to provide meaningful opportunities for emerging songwriters while steadily building the event into the country's biggest celebration of Filipino songwriting. Throughout the evening, audiences were treated to heartfelt performances from Roli Manalo (Nakak (Gigil)), Eric Diao (Di Na Bale), Jeffrey Umol (Engkanto), Ivee Madamba (Isang Habang Buhay), Off to Aurora (Sampung Hakbang), AuxJump (Balani), Maric Gavino (Atong Gugma), Aw'te Amakeh (Dulo), Toni Panagu (Breadcrumbs), Guava (28), VEEJ (Katawang Lupa), Wyanet Nazareno (Kahidlaw), Thonzkie (Batang Gapo), Si Mau Ug J (Ugma Mamatay Ra Ta), and Maria Perion (You Bring Out the Best in Me). More than a showcase of original music, the concert became a celebration of stories, dreams, and lived experiences. Every songwriter shared a deeply personal piece of themselves through songs that reflected their unique voices and artistic journeys. Reflecting on the performances, FILSCAP Vice President Tito Cayamanda shared how meaningful the experience was even for veteran songwriters. Having heard the finalists' songs from their original demos, he witnessed how each piece evolved into a fully realized performance on stage, highlighting the remarkable creativity and musical gifts of the emerging songwriters. Adding to the excitement of the evening was a special guest performance by Angela Ken, whose appearance energized the packed venue and underscored the importance of supporting Filipino songwriting across generations. The overwhelming response to this year's event reflects the growing appreciation for original Filipino music and the increasing recognition of the people behind the songs. With its record attendance, expanded production, and nationwide search for talent, Songwriters' Night Select has firmly established itself as the biggest celebration of Filipino songwriters in the country. It is a stage where emerging composers are not only discovered, but celebrated as the future of OPM. As the night came to a close, FILSCAP announced that Songwriters' Night Select will return in 2027, promising an even bigger celebration of Filipino songwriting. The organization also revealed that its Songwriters' Night Open Mic Series will once again travel across the Philippines next year, visiting different cities and communities in search of the next generation of songwriters who will one day take the Music Museum stage. Through these continuing initiatives, FILSCAP remains steadfast in its mission to discover, nurture, and champion Filipino music creators, ensuring that the future of OPM begins with the songwriters themselves.

Crimea strikes could rise sevenfold if Western funds came faster, Ukraine drone commander tells AP. EASTERN UKRAINE (AP) — The commander leading Ukraine’s drone war says his country’s recent strikes in Crimea are the first phase of a campaign aimed at rendering the peninsula — illegally annexed by Russia in 2014 — unusable as a staging ground for Russian forces. Maj. Robert “Magyar” Brovdi, one of Ukraine’s most prominent commanders among a new generation of soldiers, said his forces could strike seven times more military targets in Crimea if the money pledged by Western allies came faster. “Crimea falls within the key conceptual pillars on the path to ending the war,” Brovdi told The Associated Press in an interview. Despite that shortfall, Ukraine’s summer campaign in Crimea has already inflicted significant damage: striking rail bridges, oil depots and power infrastructure to disrupt supply lines and blind Russian air defenses as drones fly in. Brovdi said his forces are equipped at just 14% of what they would need to carry out the Crimea campaign at full capacity. A firm believer in numbers since his past life running an international grain trading business, Brovdi joined Ukraine’s territorial defense as a volunteer in the war’s opening days. He rose quickly, commanding one of the country’s most effective drone brigades before being tapped to lead a force with no precedent before this war — Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces. “It’s not that the production capacity of Ukrainian manufacturers doesn’t allow us to make the necessary quantities” of drones, Brovdi said. “It’s the banal problem of untimely financing, which our partners do allocate, but which moves significantly slower than our plans.” A lover of the arts A devoted patron of the arts, Brovdi's underground command post resembles a museum, with pieces of Ukrainian art on display, including by renowned painter Maria Prymachenko — each with small placards noting their titles and a QR code linking to more information. “Please don’t touch the sculpture,” reads a sign beneath one piece. The artwork sits against a backdrop of dozens of screens streaming live footage from the front, along with real-time data that drives decisions on the battlefield. Soldiers can grab good coffee, pick a book, work out or rest in sleeping pods — a culture that feels closer to a Silicon Valley office than a war room. They work around the clock to try to prevent Crimea from functioning as a staging ground for the Russian military, said Brovdi, whose call sign, Magyar, nods to his ethnic Hungarian roots in Zakarpattia, the western Ukrainian region bordering Hungary. He pointed to one sign of progress — in four recent large-scale Russian missile barrages from the peninsula, only five missiles were launched in total, a drop he credited to the systematic destruction of Russian air defenses there. The AP couldn’t independently verify the claim. To open that “window” for drones to strike the peninsula without being shot down en masse, his forces destroyed more than 300 air defense assets over recent months — surface-to-air systems, radar stations, electronic warfare equipment. The window metaphor sends him into a sidetrack about something personal — he loves sleeping with one open, a pleasure he rarely gets anymore as one of Russia’s most hunted men, who spends most of his time in underground bunkers. Forcing Russia out of Crimea Much of Russia's Soviet-era air defense hardware runs on the power grid, which is one of the reasons Crimea's electrical infrastructure has become a recurring target. Russian soldiers become “blind,” left with just machine guns and rifles, he said. The tactic has also impacted access to power for civilians, and Brovdi said he has twice publicly apologized to Ukrainians living in Crimea for the disruptions. Wherever Starlink connectivity reaches across Crimea, his forces can now destroy even the most heavily defended target using an average of just three drones, mixing munitions with different characteristics and warheads depending on what’s being hit. He described the strikes as deliberately calibrated — different munitions for a bridge pier than for a fuel truck or a moving train — and said his forces avoid hitting civilian infrastructure. “Creating conditions that make it impossible for any kind of military capability … to remain there will make Crimea uninteresting ... as a military staging ground,” he said. Ukraine is also working to dismantle Crimea’s role as a naval base — a blow to Russia’s presence near NATO’s borders, he added. The campaign’s early results have not been made public, Brovdi said. But roughly two weeks into the offensive that began in late June, he said Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russian authorities had ordered all military commands and security services to relocate off the peninsula, along with a covert order to remove secret archives and artworks. The AP could not independently verify the account. Threats from Russia Meanwhile, Russia is working to counter Ukraine’s edge. It is installing jamming systems at a scale that will, to some degree, degrade Starlink connectivity, Brovdi said. Russia is also building its own satellite communications system to rival Starlink, he said. “This is a risk for the entire planet,” Brovdi said, “because a dictatorship will gain access to information across the whole globe.” He also pointed to other threats facing Ukraine. The concentration of jet-powered Shahed drones, which are much harder for Ukraine to shoot down, has increased two and a half times in recent weeks, he said. Russia's military can currently fire a simultaneous salvo of 77 ballistic missiles, he said, and plans to increase that to 200. That is one of Ukraine’s most vulnerable points, since the country is running short of interceptors for the U.S.-made Patriot — the only system Ukraine has in its arsenal against ballistic missiles — meaning dozens fired by Russia during mass barrages get through and hit their targets. “Even if they only manage half of that, it will all be flying at us,” Brovdi said. The only way to bring the number down, he said, is by striking every facility involved in producing those missiles — underscoring the importance of Ukraine’s long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory. Ukraine's plan for Russia's Wildberries Ukraine has increasingly targeted Wildberries, Russia’s largest online marketplace sometimes described as the country’s answer to Amazon, and Brovdi named it as a target. “Wildberries is, first of all, a supply platform — it’s the war’s quartermaster,” he said, noting the company runs a dedicated section selling goods for Russia’s military. At the same time, he said, the strikes on the retail chain are meant to make ordinary Russians feel the war directly, in hopes the resulting desire to end it could weigh on Russia’s ability to keep fighting. Brovdi declined to give a timeline for the Wildberries campaign, saying only that the strikes will continue “until it becomes impossible for it to recover quickly.” “Ultimately, Wildberries is, forgive the expression, a consumer gambling addiction,” he said, arguing that losing access to it — like restrictions on social media — creates an intrusion on one's personal life that most Russians feel. “It turned out to be a sensitive sensor of the comfort of Russia’s massive population — people who consider themselves completely untouched by the actions of the aggressor country," he said.

Death toll from heavy rains rises to 15; PNP says 6 more missing. The death toll from the heavy rains due to tropical cyclones in the past days but are continuously being induced by southwest monsoon rose to 15 in the updated reports from the Philippine National Police (PNP). PNP spokesman Col. Allen Rae Co said a total of six people were also reported missing while 13 were injured due to different incidents that include landslides, flashflood, and electrocution. “All of these are still to be validated by the Office of Civil Defense but these are the reports that we obtained from our personnel on the ground,” said Co in a press briefing at Camp Crame in Quezon City. In Ilocos Region, one person was reported to have been electrocuted in La Union while another one drowned in Alaminos, Pangasinan. In Cordillera Administrative Region, six people died due to two separate incidents of landslides—two of them died in La Trinidad, Benguet last week while four more died in Baguio City on Sunday night. In Calabarzon, seven people were reported fatalities— three of them from Batangas due to drowning, electrocution and landslide; two due to landslides in Rodriguez, Rizal; one in Binangonan, Rizal due to drowning; and another one in Antipolo City who was hit by an uprooted tree. PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio C. Nartatez, Jr. earlier ordered the mobilization of more policemen and resources to assist local government units in disaster respose as heavy rains continue. On Monday, Nartatez gave another order alerting police units in areas affected by heavy rains to prepare for preemptive evacuation, especially that some dams released waters after reaching critical levels. Co said more than 3,300 policemen were already deployed to secure vital installations and evacuees staying in various evacuation centers across the country. Weather experts warned that the heavy rains will continue at least on Tuesday. In Mimaropa, police forces further increased their operational readiness as the “habagat” continues to bring heavy rains across parts of the region. Brig. Gen. Christopher dela Cruz, director of the Police Regional Office-Mimaropa, said police units have been instructed to closely monitor vulnerable areas, maintain coordination with local government units (LGUs) and disaster risk reduction and management offices, and ensure the immediate availability of personnel and resources whenever the situation requires. He said Regional Standby Support Force (RSSF) personnel have been placed on standby across the region for immediate deployment and augmentation. Mimaropa is composed of the provinces of Occidental and Oriental Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon and Palawan. Del Cruz said police personnel were positioned at evacuation centers, transport hubs, and other areas of concern to assist affected and stranded individuals, maintain peace and order, and help keep communities safe. “Our priority is to make sure that our people and resources are ready before they are needed, especially in areas where the weather may pose a threat to life and property,” said Dela Cruz. In Western Visayas, police forces have shifted to road clearing as part of the efforts to normalize the daily activities after the heavy rains blocked some road networks. Brig. Gen. Randulf T. Tuaño, director of the Police Regional Office 6, said police commanders were instructed to monitor blocked road networks and ensure that they are all cleared. He said coordination was also done to check on the condition of local residents in areas heavily affected by the weather disturbance. “The objective of these operations is to ensure the smooth flow of traffic and to improve the mobility of residents, rescue teams and other responders in order for all the government to reach the affected residents in the soonest possible time,” said Tuaño.

More than negligence! Quimbo seeks House probe on non-working Marikina pumping stations. Wasting no time, Marikina City 2nd district Rep. Miro Quimbo has formally sought a congressional inquiry into the non-operation of the Tumana and Iwahig pumping stations during the onslaught of the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat. Quimbo filed House Resolution (HR) No. 1342 on Monday, Aug. 10, a day after he personally led inspections at the these pumping stations only to discover them unattended and not working. The resolution directed the appropriate House committee to conduct an inquiry in aid of legislation to determine the cause of the pumping stations’ non-operation and establish accountability for the contractor and operator, J.D. Legaspi Construction. “This is precisely when flood-control infrastructure should be working—not sitting idle or unattended while our people are facing rising floodwaters,” Quimbo said. “This incident is more than just negligence, this is blatant betrayal of public trust,” said the House Committee on Ways and Means chairman. The measure noted that Barangay Tumana, the second-most populated barangay in Marikina City with 49,950 residents, has historically been among the communities most vulnerable to flooding. The Tumana and Iwahig pumping stations were established by the Department of Public Works and Highways-Unified Project Management Office (DPWH-UPMO) to help manage and reduce flooding in Tumana and adjacent communities, particularly during intense rainfall and rising water levels in the Marikina River. However, residents reported on Aug. 9 that the two pumping stations were not functioning as floodwaters entered streets and homes. Following the reports, an on-site inspection found that the facilities appeared non-operational and unattended, with no personnel of construction company present at the site. Quimbo's displeasure was evident as he reported his findings on Facebook live Sunday afternoon. He said the situation raises serious questions regarding the contractor’s compliance with its obligations, the adequacy of DPWH UPMO oversight, the reliability of maintenance arrangements, and the readiness of flood-control infrastructure during emergencies. “What happened in Tumana raises a very basic question: when our communities needed these pumping stations the most, why were they not operating?” the veteran solon pointed out. “Flood-control infrastructure is not just another government facility. It is there to protect lives, homes, livelihoods, and property. It cannot be left unattended or neglected precisely when the flood risk is highest,” he added. Under the resolution, the House inquiry will seek to determine the cause of the non-operation of the Tumana and Iwahig pumping stations during the Aug. 9 flooding and determine the accountability of the contractor and operator. Quimbo said the investigation should not only establish what happened during but also identify measures to prevent a similar failure of flood-control infrastructure in the future.

Fuel prices cut by up to ₱4.88 per liter in major weekly rollback. Motorists and businesses are set to receive relief this week as local retail fuel prices record significant declines, driven by lower international benchmark costs and a stronger local currency. Effective Aug. 11, local pump prices for gasoline will decline by ₱4.70 per liter, diesel by ₱4.30 per liter, and kerosene by ₱4.88 per liter, according to prescribed price adjustments announced by the Department of Energy (DOE). The price cuts reflect recent volatility in global crude markets and the strengthening the peso against the United States (US) dollar, which helped reduce import costs for local refiners and distributors. The DOE attributed the international benchmark declines to ongoing diplomatic negotiations between the US and Iran, which temporarily reduced supply risk premiums in energy markets. The DOE has not provided updated metrics regarding the nation’s current commercial oil inventory. Market analysts, however, cautioned that the pump price reductions may be short-lived. Global oil markets remain volatile after Iran refused to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, demanding the removal of US financial sanctions and compensation for war damages. The shipping choke point handles a critical portion of global crude supplies, creating persistent supply security risks.

OCD: 12 dead, 1.3M individuals affected by ‘habagat,’ tropical cyclones. (UPDATED STORY) At least 12 people have died while more than 1.3 million others have been affected by the combined effects of the enhanced southwest monsoon (habagat) and the previous tropical cyclones “Luis” and “Maymay,” the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) said Monday, Aug. 10. The latest figures as of 10 a.m. showed 384,520 families or 1,310,000 people were affected across 10 regions namely National Capital Region (NCR), Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), Ilocos (Region 1), Cagayan Valley (Region 2), Central Luzon (Region 3), Calabarzon Region 4A), Mimaropa (Region 4B), Bicol (Region 5), Western Visayas (Region 6), and Zamboanga Peninsula (Region 9). Six new fatalities were recorded, bringing the death toll to 12: four were in Baguio City due to a landslide, one in Antipolo City where a delivery rider was struck by a fallen tree, and another in Batangas City due to drowning. In Baguio City, police said 13 people were buried when a landslide struck three houses in Riverside, Guisad Surong, on Sunday, Aug. 9. As of 5:35 a.m. Monday, seven people had been extracted from the site: three were rescued alive and taken to a hospital while four were declared dead. The reported fatalities were a 17-year-old female student, two nine-year-old students, and a 56-year-old man. Six people remained missing, according to police. Previously, the OCD said two cooks were also killed in a landslide at a kitchen restaurant in La Trinidad, Benguet; two died in a rockslide in Rodriguez, Rizal; one died in Lipa, Batangas due to electrocution; and another was killed in Santa Teresita, Batangas due to a landslide. OCD Deputy Administrator for Operations, Assistant Secretary Laurence E. Mina said the reported casualties were "ongoing validation still." The OCD also recorded 11 injured individuals in CAR, Ilocos, and Calabarzon while eight persons were missing. It added that 624 evacuation centers were operating, with about 16,130 families or 58,650 people staying in them and an additional 11,360 families or 39,290 individuals were being served outside the temporary shelters. Despite the scale of the affected population, OCD spokesperson Junie Castillo said authorities had not yet seen a need for additional national resources. “For our fellow Filipinos in evacuation centers, the good thing is that our local governments, as well as national government agencies, have prepositioned food and non-food items. We have not seen any shortage,” Castillo said. “As of the latest report, no local government has requested national intervention because the regional resources that have been prepositioned are still sufficient,” he added. The weather disturbances also damaged a total of 367 houses. Of these, 340 were partially damaged and 27 were totally destroyed. Infrastructure damage was estimated at P1.12 billion while agricultural losses stood at P3.53 million. The government has provided P33.94 million in assistance to the affected communities. Flooding concerns Castillo said flooding remained a concern in several areas although government response teams had already been deployed to communities requesting assistance. “Regarding the flooded areas, there were still reported flooding incidents as of last night. For our fellow Filipinos requesting rescue, we have already deployed teams,” he said. The Search, Rescue and Retrieval (SRR) cluster of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) has deployed personnel from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), Philippine National Police (PNP), and Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) for the intensified operations. The PCG said it had evacuated 7,887 residents from affected communities in Romblon, Batangas, Cavite, Rizal, Laguna and Pampanga over the weekend. PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said the agency had deployed response teams before conditions worsened. “Almost 7,887 evacuated individuals were assisted by the PCG over the weekend. The PCG remains on heightened alert, together with its deployable response groups and floating assets,” Cayabyab said. The PCG also provided free rides to stranded commuters in Batangas and Cavite. It assisted the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) and local governments in distributing family food packs and helped clear roads of fallen debris. Cayabyab said the early evacuations helped prevent residents from being caught in the worst conditions. “We had no problems with the evacuation efforts. Our fellow Filipinos cooperated, and our operations were swift,” she said. “What was good was that there was no report of search and rescue, because that is what the PCG wants to avoid. We do not want to evacuate our fellow Filipinos only when the bad weather is already at its peak,” she added. The PCG said flooding in Cavite was particularly severe, reaching almost chest level in some areas. Narrow roads also hampered the movement of response teams and equipment, including rubber boats, into some communities. Stranded in ports The PCG also continued monitoring maritime facilities as habagat disrupted sea travel. As of 4 a.m. Monday, 20 ports were being monitored across Western Visayas, Bicol, Southern Tagalog, and Central Visayas, where 472 passengers, truck drivers, and cargo helpers were stranded, and 86 rolling cargoes were affected. Twenty-four vessels, 531 motorbancas, and three tugboats were also taking shelter because of the weather. “We advise our fellow Filipinos who intend to travel to contact the vessel company first before going to the port so they will not be stranded,” Cayabyab said. She also warned fishermen and motorbanca operators against going out to sea during dangerous conditions. “To our fellow fishermen and motorbanca operators, please do not go out to sea if there is a gale warning or bad weather in your area. Your safety is our top priority,” Cayabyab said. Funds sufficient Meanwhile, the OCD said government agencies remained prepared to respond to further weather disturbances, with more tropical cyclones possible in August. “We have not seen any indication that our funds will be insufficient, including the Quick Response Fund and budget for food and non-food items. Our response agencies also have personnel and equipment ready,” Castillo said. “In fact, heavy equipment, personnel, and other resources of our response agencies are currently on standby,” he added. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has directed government agencies and local governments to address the needs of affected communities. Castillo said the OCD, NDRRMC, and other agencies would provide the President with an update on the situation. “To our fellow Filipinos, especially those in low-lying areas, first, listen to the advisories of PAGASA and local authorities. They are the ones who can tell you what needs to be done. Follow them immediately because this is for your safety,” he said.

Goldilocks turns 60 with a gooey new chocolate cake. Goldilocks is marking its 60th anniversary with a new addition to its Luscious cake lineup, the Luscious Gooey Choco, a two-layer chocolate chiffon cake created for birthdays and other celebrations. The cake is filled and iced with creamy milk chocolate fudge frosting, then finished with light chocolate buttercream and topped with white chocolate chips arranged on rosettes. The combination is designed to deliver balanced sweetness and a soft, melt-in-your-mouth texture. So, what makes it "gooey"? The answer is the cake's milky chocolate fudge, which stays soft instead of hardening like regular icing. This gives each slice its rich, melty texture and sets the new cake apart from a more traditional chocolate-frosted cake. The Luscious Gooey Choco is available at select Goldilocks stores starting Aug. 3, with nationwide availability beginning Aug. 17. In-store prices start at P610, although prices may vary by store and delivery platform. The anniversary celebration also comes with a new birthday song from Goldilocks. The cheerful jingle encourages families to sing, clap and blow out the candles together, adding another element to the bakeshop's birthday celebrations. For Goldilocks, which has spent six decades becoming a familiar part of Filipino celebrations, the new cake offers another reason to gather around the birthday table.

'Kaka sa Yawan': Different cultures, shared brotherhood. In a nutshell, “Kaka sa Yawan” takes a simple idea and lets it breathe. In his first Cinemalaya feature, director Alpha Habon follows the friendship between Niko, a young man from Manila, and Ayan, a Tadyawan Mangyan boy. Played by Beaver Magtalas and Benedix Ramos, with Queenay also in the cast, the two lead us into a story about friendship that slowly crosses the lines of culture and circumstance. They may come from very different worlds, but they share many of the same hopes, dreams and desire for a better life. The film is at its best when it simply observes the two characters and their growing bond. Habon does not force the cultural differences into a lesson. He lets the relationship develop naturally, helped by restrained performances and Patrick Rodil’s beautiful but unshowy cinematography of Mindoro. There are parts that could have been tighter, especially when the pace starts to drag. Still, the film’s sincerity carries it through. What makes “Kaka sa Yawan” appealing is its simplicity. It finds something familiar in the friendship of two people who grew up in very different circumstances. There is warmth in watching them understand each other, and a quiet happiness in seeing their friendship take shape. For a first feature, Habon has made a modest but thoughtful film, one that finds its strength in its characters and the bond they form. “Kaka sa Yawan” is currently showing in cinemas as part of the 22nd Cinemalaya Philippine Independent Film Festival, running from August 7 to 16.

Jeongyeon leaves JYP Entertainment to pursue acting career. K-pop idol Jeongyeon has parted ways with JYP Entertainment to pursue an acting career, but she will remain a member of TWICE. In a letter posted on Instagram, Jeongyeon announced that she is "now preparing to start a new chapter in a new place." She thanked JYP Entertainment for its support and assured fans that TWICE will remain her top priority. "Standing before ONCE as a member of TWICE will always be my very first priority," she wrote. "I will prepare step by step with all my heart, both for my journey as TWICE's Jeongyeon, whom you have loved so much, and for the new challenges ahead as Yu Jeongyeon." Jeongyeon is the first TWICE member to part ways with JYP Entertainment after all nine members renewed their contracts with the agency in 2022. Following her departure from JYP Entertainment, Jeongyeon has joined Varo Entertainment, the agency that also represents her older sister, actress Gong Seung-yeon. Varo Entertainment confirmed that it has signed Jeongyeon to an exclusive contract for her acting activities. "We are truly delighted to form a precious relationship with Yu Jeongyeon, who possesses diverse charms and infinite potential," the agency said.

PNVF elects new officers. Frank Lao was elected president of the Philippine National Volleyball Federation (PNVF) on Monday, Aug. 10, at the Solaire Theater Southlinks Boardroom 2M. Also elected were Atty. Donn Kapunan (vice president), Rommel Ng (treasurer), POC secretary-general Atty. Wharton Chan (auditor) and board of trustees Sienna Olaso, Francis Chad Salimbangon, Carmela Gamboa, Rustico Camangian, Mohamad Bernan Jr. and Jonas Cabochan. Asian Volleyball Confederation president Ramon “Tats” Suzara, the first PNVF president, was also elected to the board while Donaldo Caringal was appointed secretary-general. The three others on the 13-member board -- Philippine Olympic Committee (POC) appointed and a male and female representative from the athletes’ commission—will be announced soon. FIVB appointed Ad Hoc Committee chair Hila Asanuma of Palau and FIVB External Legal Consultant Atty. Alexa Monica Dabao witnessed and certified the exercise. With the development, the POC relinquished its role as “caretaker” of the federation which was mandated by volleyball’s world governing body, FIVB, following the PNVF suspension a few months ago.

Robin Padilla pushes jail time, fine for giving fake subpoena addresses. Sen. Robinhood “Robin” Padilla is seeking to penalize individuals who deliberately provide false addresses to prevent respondents from receiving subpoenas and allow preliminary investigations to proceed without their participation. Under Senate Bill No. 1957, Padilla proposed imprisonment of six months to two years and a fine of P100,000 to P300,000 for anyone who intentionally gives a false address to facilitate a preliminary investigation conducted ex parte. Padilla said a preliminary investigation, while not yet a trial, can already expose a person to public accusations and the financial, emotional, and personal burdens associated with criminal prosecution. “Karapatan ng bawat Pilipino ang mabigyan ng pagkakataong malaman at sagutin ang mga paratang laban sa kanya. Hindi dapat magamit ang maling address bilang paraan upang maisagawa ang preliminary investigation nang hindi man lamang nabibigyan ng pagkakataong makaharap at makasagot ang respondent (It is the right of every Filipino to be allowed to know and answer the allegations against them. A false address should not be used as a means to conduct a preliminary investigation without allowing the respondent to appear and respond to the allegations)," Padilla said. In the bill’s explanatory note, Padilla cited the due process guarantee under the 1987 Constitution, which requires compliance with legally established procedures before a person may be deprived of life, liberty or property. He said the proposed measure would also help prevent government resources from being wasted on prosecutions that are pursued without properly notifying the respondent. “Hindi lamang respondent ang naaagrabyado kapag sinadyang gumamit ng maling address. Nasasayang din ang oras at resources ng ating justice system. Dapat may pananagutan ang sinumang sadyang gumagawa nito upang malusutan ang tamang proseso (It is not only the respondent who is disadvantaged when a false address is deliberately used. The time and resources of our justice system are also wasted. Anyone who deliberately does this to circumvent due process should be held accountable)," Padilla said. Under the bill, a preliminary investigation is intended to determine whether there is sufficient basis to establish that a crime may have been committed and that the respondent is probably guilty and should face trial. Padilla said Senate Bill No. 1957 ultimately seeks to strengthen due process protections against malicious or oppressive prosecution while preserving the integrity of the preliminary investigation process.

DSWD has P6-B standby funds, 4.98 million food packs prepositioned nationwide. The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) on Monday, Aug. 10, said it has P6 billion in standby funds and more than 4.98 million family food packs (FFPs) prepositioned nationwide as it continues to assist those affected by the enhanced southwest monsoon or “habagat’ and tropical cyclones “Luis” and “Maymay.” According to DSWD Disaster Response Management Group (DRMG) Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao, the agency continues to produce FFPs every day at its major warehouses in Luzon and Visayas to maintain its stockpile and keep relief supplies ready for immediate deployment during disasters. “At present we have [close to] five million family food packs prepositioned in more than a thousand warehouses across the country,” Dumlao, who is also the spokesperson of the DSWD, said during a television interview. “Every day nag-pro-produce pa rin kami ng family food packs sa Luzon Disaster Resource Center and sa Visayas Disaster Resources Center (Every day, we continue to produce family food packs at the Luzon Disaster Resource Center and the Visayas Disaster Resource Center),” she added. Under the Buong Bansa Handa (BBH) program, Dumlao said the DSWD partners with large groceries, supermarkets, and other private-sector entities through framework agreements to strengthen its disaster response supply chain. This allows the agency to preposition relief goods even in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDAs), she added. “Dahil doon sa programa natin na Buong Bansa Handa program, we are able to preposition goods doon sa mga areas that are hazard prone (Through our Buong Bansa Handa program, we are able to preposition goods in hazard-prone areas),” the spokesperson said. “Kaya nga up to the last miles sa mga geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas ay mayroon tayong warehouses at may mga goods tayo na naka-prepositioned (Even in the last-mile communities in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, we have warehouses and prepositioned relief goods).” The DSWD reported that as of 6 a.m. on Aug. 10, it had provided affected families and individuals with 54,370 FFPs, 2,722 RTEF boxes, and 1,376 NFIs. As such, the agency said it extended P928,000 in financial aid through the AICS program Dumlao underscored that the DSWD continues to monitor the situation and coordinate with local government units (LGUs) to determine the needs of affected communities. “Ang instruction po ni Secretary Rex Gatchalian ay makipag-coordinate sa mga local stakeholders to ensure that all the needed assistance are provided (Secretary Rex Gatchalian instructed us to coordinate with local stakeholders to ensure that all the necessary assistance is provided),” she said. Meanwhile, the spokesperson said volunteers may help the DSWD repack FFPs as the agency continues to replenish its relief stockpile amid the ongoing weather disturbances. “Bukas po ang Luzon Disaster Resource Center at ang Visayas Disaster Resource Center para sa mga nagnanais na tumulong sa pag-repack ng mga family food packs (The Luzon Disaster Resource Center and the Visayas Disaster Resource Center are open to those who wish to help repack family food packs),” she said. “Kung mayroon pong nagnanais na tumulong, maari lang pong magtungo sa LDRC [sa Pasay City] o VDRC diyan po sa Mandaue City (Those who wish to help may proceed to the LDRC in Pasay City or the VDRC in Mandaue City).”

Luzon gets nearly a month’s rain in just 9 days — PAGASA chief. Parts of Luzon have received nearly a month’s worth of normal rainfall in just nine days due to the passage of tropical cyclones and the enhancement of the southwest monsoon (habagat), the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Monday, Aug. 10. PAGASA Administrator Dr. Nathaniel Servando said heavy rains over the past week were brought by Tropical Depression Luis, Tropical Storm Maymay, and the enhanced habagat. Typhoon Dolphin also contributed to the persistence of the rains despite remaining outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR). “The past week nakakaranas tayo ng malakas na mga pag-ulan. Dulot ito ng Bagyong Luis at Maymay at pinag-ibayong habagat. Maging ang Bagyong Dolphin na kahit na malayo sa labas ng Philippine Area of Responsibility ay naka-impluwensiya upang ma-sustain ang mga pag-ulan hanggang sa araw na ito (Over the past week, we have been experiencing heavy rains. These were caused by Tropical Storm Luis and Maymay and the enhanced southwest monsoon. Even Typhoon Dolphin, although far outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility, influenced the situation and helped sustain the rains until today),” the PAGASA chief said. Servando said PAGASA rainfall data showed that western parts of the country, particularly Luzon, had received significant amounts of rain since the start of August. In Benguet, rainfall from Aug. 1 to 9 reached 1,413 millimeters, compared with the station’s normal August rainfall of 963 millimeters. “So halos isa't kalahating buwang ulan ang binuhos sa siyam na araw lamang (So nearly one and a half months’ worth of rain fell in just nine days),” Servando said. Zambales also recorded nearly a month’s worth of its normal August rainfall during the same period. PAGASA’s monitoring station in Iba, Zambales recorded 957 millimeters of rain from Aug. 1 to 9, compared with the normal August rainfall of 929 millimeters, or about 103 percent of the monthly normal. Servando said even Metro Manila received a substantial portion of its normal August rainfall in just nine days, as the PAGASA Science Garden station in Quezon City recorded 501.6 millimeters of rain from Aug. 1 to 9, compared with the normal August rainfall of 568 millimeters. “So almost 90 percent, nearly isang buwan ding ulan ang binuhos dito sa Quezon City in Metro Manila (So almost 90 percent, nearly a month’s worth of rain also fell here in Quezon City in Metro Manila),” he added. Servando said the weather is expected to gradually improve starting Tuesday, Aug. 11. “We expect starting tomorrow ang mga pag-ulan at lugar na maaapektuhan ng malakas na pag-ulan ay mabawasan at gradually mag-iimprove na ang ating weather starting tomorrow until Wednesday (We expect that starting tomorrow, the rains and the areas affected by heavy rainfall will decrease, and our weather will gradually improve starting tomorrow until Wednesday),” he said. OVP delivers relief aid to families affected by habagat flooding in Ilocos Norte. The Office of the Vice President (OVP) on Monday, Aug. 10, said it delivered immediate relief assistance to more than 4,000 families affected by flooding caused by the southwest monsoon, or “habagat,” in Ilocos Norte. From Aug. 3 to 7, the OVP said its Disaster Operations Center (OVP DOC) conducted disaster relief operations in the province to assist families affected by flooding brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon and Tropical Cyclone Kiyapo. The OVP said relief assistance was distributed to nearly 1,200 families in Paoay, 1,330 families in Batac City, and 1,500 families in Dingras. The relief operations were carried out as communities in parts of Ilocos Norte dealt with the effects of heavy rains and flooding associated with the weather disturbances. The OVP said the initiative was part of its continuing disaster response efforts to provide immediate assistance to Filipinos affected by calamities. The office added that it aims to ensure that no family is left behind during times of need. “Sa gitna ng mga pagsubok na dulot ng kalamidad, nananatiling katuwang ng bawat Pilipino ang OVP sa paghahatid ng maagap, makatao, at may malasakit na serbisyo, upang matiyak na walang pamilyang maiiwan sa oras ng pangangailangan (In the midst of challenges brought by calamities, the OVP remains a steadfast partner of every Filipino in delivering prompt, humane, and compassionate service, ensuring that no family is left behind in times of need),” the OVP said. The OVP has continued to deploy its disaster response operations to areas affected by natural disasters, providing relief assistance to communities in need of immediate support.

Belle and Paper offers art piece journals specially for stationery lovers in the US. Driven by digital fatigue and the desire to disconnect from screens, journaling is finding a renewed place in everyday life, particularly among younger consumers looking for more personal and tactile ways to express themselves. Market Intelo reports that the bullet journaling market is valued at nearly $1 billion and is expected to grow at an annual rate of 6.8 percent, with Asia Pacific holding the largest market share, followed by Europe and the Americas. The demand extends beyond bullet journals. Research and Markets reports that the paper notebook market is valued at $82.2 billion in 2026, covering notebooks used for education, work, journaling, planning, and creative writing. Among the factors driving the market is the growing interest of Gen Z and millennials in high-end artisan notebooks as both lifestyle pieces and tools for personal wellbeing. For Filipino artist Belle Johnson, this growing appreciation for physical stationery became the inspiration behind Belle and Paper, a journaling and stationery brand she started after moving to the US. “I've always loved art, and ever since I was little, it has been my dream to have my own business one day,” she tells Manila Bulletin Lifestyle. Her love for handwritten letters, painting, and journaling eventually led her to create the kind of journal she could not find herself. Instead of settling for an existing design, she painted her own cover. That first hand-painted journal became the beginning of Belle and Paper. Since then, Belle has sold hundreds of journals to people around the world, turning her artwork into something people can incorporate into their everyday lives.“My name is Belle, but it also means beauty. My goal has always been simple, to bring a little beauty into someone's day through art and stationery,” she says. She describes her artistic style as soft, feminine, and inspired by nature. Working primarily with watercolor, oil painting, and digital art, she draws inspiration from flowers, fairy tales, gardens, and quiet places. Her art has also evolved beyond the canvas. She has transformed her paintings into journals, bookmarks, notepads, greeting cards, and other stationery. “Seeing people actually use my artwork every day has been one of the most rewarding parts of this journey,” she says. Behind the dreamy aesthetic, however, is the reality of building a creative business. Johnson admits that balancing her artistic practice with marketing, social media, packing orders, and answering emails is something she is still learning. “Creating the product is the easy part for me. Selling it is the hard part,” she says. The experience has taught her patience, particularly during slow sales. Instead of taking it personally when people admire her work but do not purchase it, she has learned that they may simply not be ready or may not be her customers. For young creatives hoping to turn their passions into businesses, Johnson keeps her advice simple: “Just start.” “Don't wait until everything is perfect because you'll probably be waiting forever,” she says. Today, Belle and Paper is also deeply connected to her personal journey. Looking ahead, Belle is preparing to launch Belle & Paper on Amazon and hopes to work with local coffee shops and bookstores in Clarksville, Tennessee. She also dreams of seeing her artwork displayed in museums and eventually opening a shop where people can browse stationery and feel inspired to create. As a Filipina artist building her business in the United States, she hopes Belle and Paper can continue to bring creativity, encouragement, and a little beauty to people's everyday lives.

Rojo breaks through, Reig stays hot in IM 70.3 Lapu-Lapu. LAPU-LAPU CITY – Nicole Rojo announced her arrival as a rising force in Philippine triathlon, emerging as the first Filipina finisher in the IRONMAN 70.3 Lapu-Lapu while multi-titled Irienold Reig Jr. continued his remarkable run of form with another age-group victory in Cebu here last Sunday, Aug. 9. Rojo, who has built her credentials through a string of victories in smaller endurance races, finally delivered a breakthrough performance on a major stage, clocking 5:15:27 over the grueling 1.9-km swim, 90-km bike and 21-km run course. She got off to a strong start in the swim and sustained her charge through the bike and run legs, posting split times of 19:16 in the swim, 2:59:38 on the bike and 1:49:37 in the run. The performance enabled the South Cotabato native to pull away from Melona Yucot, who finished in 6:06:54, and Rachel Wong (7:38:52) to dominate the women’s 18-24 age-group division in the 12th staging of the premier endurance race presented by Megaworld and organized by Sunrise Events Inc. Reig, meanwhile, further cemented his status as one of the country’s most promising young triathletes, ruling the men’s 18-24 division in 4:23:03. He beat Dutchman Rik Beugel, who clocked 4:34:28, while fellow Filipino Eryk Omandam placed third in 4:45:41. The victory came months after Reig also topped the IRONMAN 70.3 Davao, giving further weight to the Quezon City standout’s emergence as a potential next big name in Philippine triathlon. His back-to-back victories also underscored the consistency of his form against strong fields. Jewin Ochea provided another local highlight, capturing the Elite Category title put up by the Philippine Sports Commission in 4:26:10. The race drew more than 1,400 triathletes from 48 countries, with South Africa’s Henri Schoeman and Natalie Van Coevorden of Australia taking the professional men’s and women’s titles, respectively. Schoeman captured his second title in the event, while Van Coevorden won for the first time. Beyond Rojo and Reig, however, foreign athletes stamped their class across the other age-group divisions, underscoring the depth of international competition in this year’s race. Strong currents forced organizers to shorten the swim leg for the age-group divisions from the scheduled 1.9 kilometers to one kilometer. Japan’s Kazuhiro Oishi topped the men’s 25-29 division in 4:03:39, beating Frenchmen Fabien Celeste (4:10:07) and Sebastien Refane (4:19:12). Multi-titled Bea Quiambao ruled the women’s side in 5:22:12, ahead of Aira Lopez (5:37:02) and Cynthia Ras (5:39:54). Another Japanese standout, Maeda Ryosuke, topped the men’s 30-34 division in 3:56:26, beating Julian Teves (4:26:36) and Mervin Santiago (4:29:48). Canada’s Casey Logan claimed the women’s crown in 5:20:59, ahead of Nicole Andaya (5:30:34) and Pauline Fornea (5:34:35). Hong Kong’s Ho Tin Kwok ruled the men’s 35-39 division in 4:34:40, beating Britain’s Matthew Gibson (4:40:06) and Junrey Cabarrubias (5:55:20). Malaysia’s Eva Wong took the women’s title in 5:21:25, edging Japan’s Yui Matsumoto (5:23:30) and ultrawoman Jennifer Uy (5:50:15). Other age-group winners were Japan’s Ryosute Ohata (4:12:51) and Yuko Takahashi (5:16:35) in the 40-44 divisions; Germany’s Andreas Wuestenberg (4:57:03) and Ines Santiago (5:20:54) in the 45-49 categories; Singapore-based Australian Assad Attamimi (4:19:07) and Japan’s Masami Suzuki (5:46:15) in the 50-54 divisions; Dutchman Marnix Beugel (4:40:13) and Australia’s Michelle Boyes (5:37:11) in the 55-59 categories; and Britain’s David Boyes (5:33:20) and Celma Hitalia (5:59:19) in the 60-64 divisions. Japan’s Yoshihisa Takase topped the men’s 65-69 division in 5:36:40, while compatriot Toshikazu Kobayashi won the 70-74 category in 6:41:21.

Wildfire in Indonesian national park grows. JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesia sent airplanes and hundreds of firefighters on Sunday to fight a blaze in a popular national park, one of a growing number of wildfires the country is battling during an unusually dry season. The largest fire reported this week has burned about 176 hectares (435 acres) of Mount Bromo, located within the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java province, one of Indonesia’s best-known tourist destinations. Authorities closed the park to visitors Saturday and Rudijanta Tjahja Nugraha, the park chief, said the shutdown would remain in effect until further notice. Hundreds of firefighters, disaster management personnel, police, soldiers, park rangers and volunteers have been mobilized to contain the blaze. Helicopters and drones have also been deployed to help battle the fire, while crews have built firebreaks to try to prevent further spread. Nugraha said difficult terrain has complicated efforts, with some hotspots located on steep volcanic slopes that are difficult to reach by land. The Bromo fire comes as several other wildfires have been reported across Indonesia during an unusually dry season. A forest and land fire broke out in Central Java’s Banyumas Regency on Friday, authorities said. That fire was triggered by land-clearing activities and spread rapidly to surrounding areas, fueled by dry conditions. In West Java, a fire broke out this week in the Suryakencana Meadow area of Mount Gede Pangrango National Park, a popular hiking destination. The incident prompted authorities to temporarily close hiking trails to Mount Gede and Mount Pangrango. Indonesia’s Meteorological, Climatological and Geophysical Agency said strong winds and extremely dry vegetation are accelerating the spread of fires. The El Niño weather pattern, combined with seasonal dry winds from Australia, has increased the risk of fires across parts of the country. Forest fires on Sumatra and Borneo islands often break out during dry spells. Fires are often started illegally by plantation owners or traditional farmers to clear land for planting, and those burns periodically blanket parts of Southeast Asia in hazardous haze.

Gary V gives new life to OFW favorite 'Babalik Ka Rin'. For generations of Filipinos, “Babalik Ka Rin” has been more than a Gary Valenciano hit. The song has become closely associated with the lives of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) and their families, capturing the longing, sacrifice and hope that come with leaving home to build a better life. Now, more than three decades after it was first released, Gary V is giving the OPM favorite a new rendition. The 2026 version retains the emotional pull of the original while giving it a fresh sound and feel. Gary’s familiar voice brings a different weight to a song that has remained relevant to Filipinos who know what it means to leave home and to those waiting for them to return. Originally composed and produced by Louie Ocampo, with lyrics by Dudu Ulep, “Babalik Ka Rin” was introduced in the early 1990s and eventually became one of Valenciano’s signature songs. Its connection to OFW life has only grown through the years. For many Filipinos working abroad, the song mirrors the experience of leaving loved ones behind, enduring the loneliness of being away and holding on to the promise of coming home. The new version comes with a music video that follows the realities of overseas Filipino life, from long work hours and difficult conditions to missed family milestones and the quiet moments of homesickness. It also features actual homecoming videos submitted by Filipinos from different parts of the world, showing the hugs, tears and reunions that make the journey worthwhile. For Gary, returning to “Babalik Ka Rin” was also a chance to revisit a song that has remained close to Filipino listeners. “For more than 30 years, ‘Babalik Ka Rin’ has held a special place in the hearts of Filipinos, especially our Overseas Filipinos,” Gary said. “I hope this new version reminds them that every sacrifice has meaning, every goodbye carries hope, and no matter how far life takes them, home and the people they love will always be waiting.” The new recording was made for Sendwave’s “Between Here And Home” campaign, which centers on the experiences of Filipinos living and working abroad. But beyond the campaign, the return of “Babalik Ka Rin” gives music fans a chance to hear one of Gary V’s enduring songs through a new recording while revisiting a piece of OPM that has long been tied to the Filipino experience of leaving home and finding a way back.

El Niño threatens food prices as Philippine inflation remains highest in region. The Philippines faces difficulty bringing inflation back within target as a strengthening El Niño threatens to damage crops and push food prices higher, with the country already posting the highest inflation rate in the region, according to Moody’s Analytics. In an Aug. 7 report, Moody’s Analytics noted that Philippine headline inflation eased to 6.2 percent year-on-year in July from 6.4 percent in June, but remained above the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) two- to four-percent target range. Among six Asia-Pacific economies that released July consumer price index (CPI) data last week, the Philippines recorded the strongest inflation despite the slowdown from June. Vietnam’s July inflation stood at 4.5 percent, followed by Indonesia at 2.9 percent, South Korea at 2.8 percent, and Taiwan at 2.5 percent. Thailand had the lowest rate at 1.9 percent, down from 2.4 percent in June. Moody’s Analytics cited that food prices in the Philippines increased 5.3 percent year-on-year in July, while utility prices soared 8.2 percent, and transport prices surged 11.9 percent. Meanwhile, July core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy items, eased to 4.2 percent from 4.4 percent last June. “The inflation outlook will largely depend on how developments in the Middle East alter global commodity prices,” Moody’s Analytics said. It added that the prolonged dry spell due to El Niño “poses a significant risk,” as hotter and drier conditions in the coming months could hurt crops and drive up food prices. The threat extends across the region, with Moody ’s Analytics citing a United Nations (UN) World Food Program (WFP) warning that a strengthening El Niño could leave an estimated 8.2 million additional people in Asia-Pacific facing acute food insecurity as hot and dry weather hampers planting seasons and harvests. Moody’s Analytics noted that the previous El Niño episode from late 2023 to early 2024 contributed to higher food inflation in the Philippines, India, and Indonesia. The renewed inflation threat comes as the Philippine economy is also grappling with its weakest growth since the Covid-19 pandemic. Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth slowed to 2.3 percent year-on-year in the second quarter from 2.8 percent in the first quarter, marking the weakest performance since the first quarter of 2021, when the economy contracted during the depths of the pandemic. On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, GDP growth likewise slowed to 0.6 percent from 0.9 percent. Moody’s Analytics attributed the broader slowdown partly to weak domestic demand, as private consumption growth decelerated for the fifth consecutive quarter while private investment fell sharply from a year ago. Stronger exports and higher government spending nonetheless cushioned the economic slowdown, Moody’s Analytics noted. Earlier, state weather bureau Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) officially raised the alert status to an active El Niño, warning that a severe “super El Niño” is likely to develop late in 2026 with an 81-percent probability and persist into the following year. This poses a threat to the country’s food supply, with the Department of Agriculture (DA) warning that a severe dry period could cause a 20- to 30-percent decline in rice yields, equivalent to more than half a million metric tons (MT) of rice. - Danielle T. Las Piñas gov’t assures nutrition support for typhoon-hit families. The Las Piñas City government provided emergency nutrition services to 736 families or 2,886 individuals who sought shelter in evacuation centers following the recent typhoon. Mayor April Aguilar said the city government would continue to ensure that the nutritional needs of vulnerable residents are addressed, particularly during disasters. Aguilar said that during emergencies, the city government make sure that families, especially children, pregnant and lactating women, senior citizens, and persons with disabilities, continue to receive the nutrition support they need. The Barangay Nutrition Cluster, composed of nutrition workers from several barangays, conducted Nutrition in Emergencies (NiE) interventions in various evacuation centers across the city. The services included rapid nutrition assessment, micronutrient supplementation, Vitamin A distribution, infant and young child feeding counseling, breastfeeding kits, deworming tablets, iodized salt and complementary food distribution, and management of acute malnutrition. Aguilar explained that among those reached were 410 children, 76 older persons, 17 PWDs, 15 pregnant women, and 21 lactating women.

Marikina LGU deploys bigger pumps to ease flooding. The Marikina City government deployed larger mobile booster pumps in Barangays Malanday and Tumana on Monday, Aug. 10, to speed up the drainage of floodwaters in affected areas. Mayor Maan Teodoro said the booster pumps were deployed through the Metro Manila Council to increase pumping capacity and help remove accumulated floodwaters more quickly. “Nag-deploy ang city government, sa pamamagitan ng Metro Manila Council, ng mas malalaking mobile booster flood pumps upang madagdagan ang pumping capacity at mapabilis ang pag-drain ng floodwater sa mga apektadong bahagi ng Barangay Malanday at Barangay Tumana (The city government, through the Metro Manila Council, deployed larger mobile booster flood pumps to increase pumping capacity and speed up the drainage of floodwaters in affected areas of Barangays Malanday and Tumana),” Teodoro said. According to the mayor, the newly deployed pumps have an estimated pumping capacity three times greater than the existing pumps installed at the Tumana Pumping Station. “Ang mga bagong dineploy na booster pump ay may tinatayang tatlong beses na mas malaking pumping capacity kumpara sa mga kasalukuyang pump na nakakabit sa Tumana Pumping Station (The newly deployed booster pumps have an estimated pumping capacity three times greater than the existing pumps installed at the Tumana Pumping Station),” she said. Teodoro said the additional pumps are expected to increase the volume of water discharged per hour and accelerate the removal of floodwaters toward the drainage outfall while clearing and pumping operations continue. On Sunday, Aug. 9, the local government alerted the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and asked the agency and its contractor to repair and make the pumping station operational. The deployment came after flooding was reported in Libis Bulelak in Barang Malanday and Creekside in Barangay Tumana. OPM Hitmen take their fight back to the stage. Is live music still viable when almost everything can now be watched online? Anyone who has been to a good concert or spent a night in a club listening to a band probably knows the answer. Watching a performance on a screen is convenient, but being there is different. You hear the music differently. You feel the crowd. You see the artists up close. There is also that element of surprise because anything can happen once the show starts. The OPM Hitmen know this well. Richard Reynoso, Rannie Raymundo and Chad Borja have spent years performing in front of audiences. They know how to work a crowd, adjust when something goes wrong and keep the show going. That is also what drew EchoJham Entertainment Productions to the veteran trio. The production house, headed by Juan Angelo Arenas, formally signed the OPM Hitmen on Aug. 8 in Quezon City. The partnership is expected to bring them more concerts and live projects. Borja sees the partnership as a good match. “They know that our strength is in doing live shows, they’re experts so, I think it’s a win-win partnership for us. They've got the means, we got the talent,” he said. For Reynoso, the partnership also means having people who are willing to support them at this point in their careers. “I feel like with EchoJham we found a home that would really help us and nurture us,” he said. “It's hard to find partners in this day and age that's willing to go out on a limb for you, lalo na nga at medyo we're not that young na. And I'm grateful for that.” The OPM Hitmen started in 2012 when Reynoso and Raymundo were invited to do a production number for a show. They enjoyed working together and eventually thought of bringing Borja into the act. There was an interesting detail. Borja and Raymundo had been rivals before. The combination worked. The group became known for its production numbers, with around 90 percent of their shows devoted to singing. They eventually received awards for Best Group and Best Concert. More than a decade later, the three singers continue to believe in the power of a live audience. And that could only be a good thing. The music business has changed. Younger artists now have streaming platforms and social media to reach listeners. Many can perform online and connect with audiences without leaving home. But these veterans are out to prove there is more to life beyond your computer or mobile screens. Raymundo for one maintained there is still nothing quite like being in the room. “Iba pa rin talaga ang experience for the audience kapag live,” he said. “Iba rin ang experience for us kasi the reaction is immediate. Alam mo kaagad if something is working or if it isn't.” That instant reaction is something performers learn to deal with over time. Sometimes a crowd loves a song. Sometimes it does not. Sometimes something goes wrong onstage and the artist has to figure out what to do next. The OPM Hitmen have been through enough shows to know how to handle those moments. That is what EchoJham is banking on. The company does not have to reinvent the group. It has to find the right venues, bring in the audiences and give the three singers the stage. Then they can take it from there.

QC involves danger-zone residents in cleanup efforts amid ‘habagat’. Quezon City is involving informal settlers living in danger zones in cleanup activities as the southwest monsoon or “habagat” brought heavy rains and strong winds to the city. The Department of Sanitation and Cleanup Works of Quezon City (DSQC) continued cleanup operations in various areas affected by the inclement weather, particularly along major roads such as G. Araneta Avenue. Through its Public Employment Services Office (PESO), the city is coordinating with informal settlers in danger zones on cleanup activities and efforts to prevent possible harm to them. The city is also working with residents, barangays, and government agencies through regular cleanup of waterways and major roads. Partnerships with barangays are being maintained to monitor roads and waterways and prevent illegal dumping. As part of efforts to protect vulnerable communities, the city is also moving street dwellers from danger zones to safer and more suitable areas. Meanwhile, the DSQC observed less litter and garbage during its cleanup operations, which it considered a welcome development amid the inclement weather. The DSQC said it would continue its partnership efforts with proactive QC residents, barangays, and government agencies to keep the city clean and orderly. The efforts continued as the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) raised an orange rainfall warning over Metro Manila, including Quezon City, based on its 12:09 p.m. advisory. Residents in low-lying areas, landslide-prone areas, and those living near rivers and creeks were urged to remain alert and prepared for possible rain and flooding. Quezon City said its rescue teams remained ready for immediate evacuation if necessary.

Court couture, not politics: Eala’s tournament outfits explained. Alex Eala has been drawing significant attention, not only in her impressive performances in the WTA Tour, but also in the color of her tennis outfits. At the Mubadala DC Open where she won her breakthrough WTA Tour singles title, Eala wore green throughout. This week at the National Bank Open in Toronto, Canada, where she finished in the Last 16 after yielding to world No. 14 and former champion Belinda Bencic, 4-6, 0-6, the Filipina wore pink or light magenta. The colors green and pink, particularly among Filipinos, carry meaning as they have become closely associated with some of the country’s biggest political names. But is Eala’s apparel related to politics at all? Certainly not. Rather, her tennis outfit is part of her endorsement deal as a global ambassador for Nike, one of the leading athletic footwear and apparel giants around the globe. There are no set rules on how many times a Nike-sponsored tennis player changes outfits during a season but mostly of them switch ahead of new tournaments. However, it is common for players under the brand to wear similar colorways, as seen with Eala alongside Japan’s Naomi Osaka, Mirra Andreeva, and China’s Zheng Qinwen, to name a few. Currently touted as one the brightest tennis stars, Eala, currently No. 20, is included in a bevy of talents that Nike partnered with and their deal started way back 2019 when the Filipina tennis ace was in the juniors level. From there, the charming lefty’s career rose with Nike continuing its support by gifting her a specialized sampaguita blossom-inspired hair tie during last year’s Wimbledon where she marked her main draw debut. Eala also visited the Nike World Headquarters in Oregon, USA earlier this year with the establishment features some of her photos among them are the iconic “History in full bloom.” A year later after her maiden Wimbledon appearance, Eala was honored by Nike anew with a visor which its back was embroidered with a Filipino phrase, "Kapag lumago, hindi na hihinto."
